arXiv:2401.04458v2 [math.AG] 15 Dec 2025

Algebraic Groups with Torsors That Are Versal for All Affine Varieties

Uriya A. First1 Address: 1University of Haifa Email address: uriya.first@gmail.com , Mathieu Florence2 Address: 2Université Paris Cité and Sorbonne Université, CNRS, IMJ-PRG, Paris Email address: mflorence@imj-prg.fr and Zev Rosengarten3 Address: 3Hebrew University Email address: zev.rosengarten@mail.huji.ac.il
Abstract.

Let kk be a field and let GG be an affine algebraic group over kk. Call a GG-torsor weakly versal for a class of kk-schemes 𝒞{\mathscr{C}} if it specializes to every GG-torsor over a scheme in 𝒞{\mathscr{C}}. A recent result of the first author, Reichstein and Williams says that for any d≥0d\geq 0, there exists a GG-torsor over a finite type kk-scheme that is weakly versal for finite type affine kk-schemes of dimension at most dd. The first author also observed that if GG is unipotent, then GG admits a torsor over a finite type kk-scheme that is weakly versal for all affine kk-schemes, and that the converse holds if char⁡k=0\Char k=0. In this work, we extend this to all fields, showing that GG is unipotent if and only if it admits a GG-torsor over a quasi-compact base that is weakly versal for all finite type regular affine kk-schemes. Our proof is characteristic-free and it also gives rise to a quantitative statement: If GG is a non-unipotent subgroup of 𝐆𝐋n{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}, then a GG-torsor over a quasi-projective kk-scheme of dimension dd is not weakly versal for finite type regular affine kk-schemes of dimension n⁡(d+1)+2n(d+1)+2. This means in particular that every such GG admits a nontrivial torsor over a regular affine (n+2)(n+2)-dimensional variety. When GG contains a nontrivial torus, we show that nontrivial torsors already exist over 33-dimensional smooth affine varieties (even when GG is special), and this is optimal in general.

In the course of the proof, we show that for every m,ℓ∈ℕ∪{0}m,\ell\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\} with ℓ≠1\ell\neq 1, there exists a smooth affine kk-scheme XX carrying an ℓ\ell-torsion line bundle that cannot be generated by mm global sections. We moreover study the minimal possible dimension of such an XX and show that it is mm, m+1m+1 or m+2m+2.

1. Introduction

Let kk be a field and let GG be an affine algebraic group over kk. Recall that a GG-torsor E→XE\to X, where XX is a kk-scheme, is said to be weakly versal if E→XE\to X specializes to every GG-torsor over any kk-field KK. When the joint image of all such specializations Spec⁡K→X\Spec K\to X is dense in XX, the torsor E→XE\to X is called versal; see [10], for instance. Versal torsors have many applications, notably to study of essential dimension and the theory of cohomological invariants, e.g., see [22] and [37]. In particular, the essential dimension of GG, denoted edk⁡(G)\ed_{k}(G), is equal to the minimal possible dimension of a kk-variety that is the base of a versal GG-torsor.

Given a class of kk-schemes 𝒞{\mathscr{C}}, let us say that a GG-torsor E→XE\to X is weakly versal for 𝒞{\mathscr{C}} if every GG-torsor over a scheme in 𝒞{\mathscr{C}} is a specialization of E→XE\to X. This definition first appeared in [14, §5], where it was shown that if kk is infinite, then for every d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}, there exists a GG-torsor over a finite type kk-scheme that is weakly versal for the class of finite type affine kk-schemes of dimension at most dd. Special examples of this phenomena were observed earlier, e.g., [31] and [2, §5.1]. Weak versality for general classes of kk-schemes, as well as stronger variants of this property, were studied systematically by the first author in [12], and we refer to introduction of this source for a more detailed history. By [12, Thm. 8.2], for every d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N} and every algebraic subgroup GG of 𝐆𝐋n{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}, there is a GG-torsor over a quasi-projective kk-scheme of dimension n​d+n2−dimGnd+n^{2}-\dim G that is versal (in the strongest sense considered in [12]) for the class of affine noetherian kk-schemes of dimension at most dd.

Perhaps more surprisingly, it was observed in [12, Thm. 10.1] that if GG is unipotent (see [23, 6.45, 14.5] for the definition), then there are GG-torsors over quasi-projective kk-schemes that are weakly versal for all affine kk-schemes.11 1 Note that in characteristic 00, every GG-torsor over an affine scheme is trivial when GG is unipotent, but in positive characteristic, unipotent groups may have nontrivial torsors. The special case where p:=char⁡k>0p:=\Char k>0 and GG is a finite constant pp-group goes back to Saltman [31]; see also [16]. The first author also showed that the converse holds in characteristic 00, that is, an algebraic kk-group admitting a GG-torsor over a finite type kk-scheme that is versal for all affine kk-schemes is unipotent [12, Thm. 10.6]. They asked whether this also holds in positive characteristic. Our first main result answers this question in the affirmative.

Theorem 1.1.

Let GG be an affine algebraic group over a field kk. Then the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (a)

    there exists a GG-torsor over a quasi-compact kk-scheme that is weakly versal for all finite type regular affine kk-schemes;

  2. (b)

    there exists a GG-torsor over a smooth quasi-projective kk-scheme that is weakly versal for all affine kk-schemes;

  3. (c)

    GG is unipotent.

Our proof is very different from the argument in [12]. It works in any characteristic, applies to torsors over a quasi-compact base (rather than of finite type over kk), and it also yields a quantitative variant for GG-torsors over quasi-projective kk-schemes, which is our second main result.

Theorem 1.2.

Let kk be a field, and let GG be a non-unipotent algebraic subgroup of the algebraic kk-group 𝐆𝐋n{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}. Let E→XE\to X be a GG-torsor such that XX is quasi-projective over a kk-field and of dimension dd. Then E→XE\to X is not weakly versal for the class of finite type regular affine kk-schemes of dimension at most n⁡(d+1)+2n(d+1)+2.

Both theorems admit mild improvements when some assumptions are imposed on GG or kk; see Section 6. For example, if GG is connected or kk is perfect, then we may replace “finite type regular” in condition (a) of Theorem 1.1 and in Theorem 1.2 with “smooth”. Furthermore, if GG contains a nontrivial torus, then we can assert in Theorem 1.2 that E→XE\to X is not versal for smooth affine kk-schemes of dimension ≤n⁡(d+1)+1\leq n(d+1)+1. The strongest statements we can make about particular GG and kk are given in Theorems 6.1 and 6.2.

Theorem 1.2 implies that every non-unipotent algebraic subgroup of 𝐆𝐋n{\mathbf{GL}}_{n} admits a nontrivial GG-torsor over a finite type regular affine kk-scheme of dimension ≤n+2\leq n+2; mild improvements of this are given in Corollaries 6.5 and 6.6. However, we can do significantly better when GG contains a nontrivial torus.

Theorem 1.3.

Let GG be an affine algebraic kk-group containing a nontrivial torus (resp. central torus). Then there exists a smooth affine kk-scheme XX of dimension ≤3\leq 3 (resp. 11) carrying a nontrivial GG-torsor. When char⁡k=0\Char k=0 and trdegℚ​k\mathrm{trdeg}_{\mathbb{Q}}k is infinite, we can take XX to be of dimension ≤2\leq 2.

Theorem 1.3 is the best result we can hope for with general kk and GG. Indeed, we show that any 𝐒𝐋n{\mathbf{SL}}_{n}-torsor (n>1n>1) over a noetherian affine scheme of dimension smaller than 22 is trivial (Example 7.3), and moreover, every 𝐒𝐋n{\mathbf{SL}}_{n}-torsor over a smooth affine 𝔽¯p\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}-scheme of dimension smaller then 33 is trivial (Corollary 7.5). The characteristic-00 analogue of the latter, i.e., that every 𝐒𝐋n{\mathbf{SL}}_{n}-torsor over a smooth affine ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}}-scheme of dimension ≤2\leq 2 is trivial, is equivalent to the Bloch–Beilinson conjecture for surfaces (Remark 7.6).

The “local” counterpart of Theorem 1.3, i.e., the problem of finding nontrivial torsors over kk-fields, was already considered by Reichstein and Youssin [30]. To put their result in context, recall that Serre made two conjectures about the triviality of torsors over fields of small cohomological dimension [35], [36, III.§3]. Serre’s Conjecture I — now a theorem of Steinberg [41] — states that if GG is a connected algebraic group over a field KK of cohomological dimension ≤1\leq 1, then every GG-torsor over KK is trivial. Serre’s Conjecture II states that if GG is a semisimple22 2 We follow the convention that reductive groups, and in particular semisimple groups, are connected. simply connected algebraic group over a perfect field KK of cohomological dimension ≤2\leq 2, then every GG-torsor over KK is trivial; this conjecture is known in many cases [19]. Serre further called an algebraic group GG over kk special if every GG-torsor over a kk-field is trivial [34]. The main result of [30], which we state here only in characteristic 00 for simplicity, informally says that Serre’s conjectures I and II are optimal. Formally, suppose that GG is an algebraic group over an algebraically closed field kk (with char⁡k=0\Char k=0). Then:

  1. (i)

    If GG is not connected, then GG has nontrivial torsors over any kk-field of transcendence degree 11.

  2. (ii)

    If G/rad⁡(G)G/\mathrm{rad}(G) is not semisimple simply connected, then GG has nontrivial torsors over any kk-field of transcendence degree 22.

  3. (iii)

    If GG is not special, then GG has nontrivial torsors over any kk-field of transcendence degree 33.

By spreading out, these statements imply a result similar to Theorem 1.3, but which applies only to non-special groups. In addition to addressing the case of special groups containing a nontrivial torus, Theorem 1.3 improves the “global” consequences of (i)–(iii) when GG is semisimple simply connected and trdegℚ​k\mathrm{trdeg}_{\mathbb{Q}}k is infinite by showing that there exist nontrivial GG-torsors over 22-dimensional smooth affine kk-schemes. (There are also additional improvements in positive characteristic.) On the other hand, the global analogue of (i) gives a better result than Theorem 1.3 for non-connected (smooth) algebraic groups.

We return to the case where GG is an affine algebraic group over some field kk. Another way to look at Theorem 1.2 is via the following corollary:

Corollary 1.4.

Let GG be an algebraic subgroup of the algebraic kk-group 𝐆𝐋n{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}, and let md​(G)m_{d}(G) be the smallest m∈ℕ∪{0}m\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\} for which there is a GG-torsor over an mm-dimensional quasi-projective kk-scheme that is weakly versal for finite type affine kk-schemes of dimension at most dd. If GG is not unipotent, then

⌊d−2n⌋≤md​(G)≤n​d+n2−dimG.\left\lfloor{\frac{d-2}{n}}\right\rfloor\leq m_{d}(G)\leq nd+n^{2}-\dim G.

Otherwise,

md​(G)≤n⁡(n−1)2−dimG.m_{d}(G)\leq\frac{n(n-1)}{2}-\dim G.
Proof.

The lower bound follows from Theorem 1.2. The upper bounds follow from [12, Thms. 8.2, 10.1] ∎

When d=0d=0, the integer md​(G)m_{d}(G) is just the essential dimension of GG,33 3 This is true despite the fact that Corollary 1.4 considers only torsors over quasi-projective kk-schemes. Indeed, we clearly have edk⁡(G)≤m0​(G)\ed_{k}(G)\leq m_{0}(G). Furthermore, if p:E→Xp:E\to X is a versal GG-torsor, then there is a versal GG-torsor E′→X′E^{\prime}\to X^{\prime} with dimX′=dimX\dim X^{\prime}=\dim X and X′X^{\prime} affine (and in particular quasi-projective) — simply take a dense open affine X′⊆XX^{\prime}\subseteq X and E′=p−1​(X′)E^{\prime}=p^{-1}(X^{\prime}). Thus, m0​(G)m_{0}(G) is smaller than min⁡{dimX|E→X is a versal G-torsor}\min\{\dim X\,|\,\text{$E\to X$ is a versal $G$-torsor}\}, which is edk⁡(G)\ed_{k}(G). so the invariants {md​(G)}d≥0\{m_{d}(G)\}_{d\geq 0} may be regarded as “higher” analogues of the essential dimension. Corollary 1.4 tells us that the sequence {md​(G)}d≥0\{m_{d}(G)\}_{d\geq 0} is either bounded — which is the case precisely when GG is unipotent — or it has linear growth rate.

We prove Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 by establishing three results.

First, we show in Theorem 3.6 that an affine algebraic kk-group GG is not unipotent if and only if Gk¯G_{\overline{k}} contains a copy of 𝝁ℓ{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell} (the group of ℓ\ell-th roots of unity) for some ℓ>1\ell>1; this was known if GG is smooth and connected [7, Ch. IV, Cor. 11.5(2)]. We also show that a general connected algebraic kk-group (possibly not affine or not smooth) that is not unipotent has a nontrivial multiplicative algebraic subgroup.

Next, we show in Theorem 4.5 that if GG is linear and contains a copy of 𝝁ℓ{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell}, and if there is a GG-torsor over a quasi-compact scheme XX that is weakly versal for a class 𝒞{\mathscr{C}} of affine kk-schemes, then there is a uniform bound on the number of generators of every ℓ\ell-torsion line bundle over a scheme in 𝒞{\mathscr{C}}. This upper bound is explicit if XX is quasi-projective over a kk-field.

Finally, we show in Theorem 5.1 that for every m,ℓ∈ℕ∪{0}m,\ell\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\} with ℓ≠1\ell\neq 1, there exists a smooth affine kk-scheme XX admitting an ℓ\ell-torsion line bundle that cannot be generated by mm global sections; such examples were known for ℓ=2\ell=2 if char⁡k≠2\Char k\neq 2 [38, Prop. 7.13, Prop. 6.3]. More generally, we study what is the minimal possible dimension of XX (also in the non-torsion case ℓ=0\ell=0) and show that it is mm, m+1m+1 or m+2m+2. A key results which we establish along the way is the following criterion (Lemma 5.4): If the mm-th power of the 11-st Chern class of a line bundle LL is nonzero, then LL cannot be generated by mm global sections.

Putting Theorems 3.6, 4.5 and 5.1 together tells us (after a little work) that if GG is not unipotent, then no GG-torsor over a quasi-compact base E→XE\to X is weakly versal for all finite type regular affine kk-schemes. This gives Theorem 1.1. When XX is quasi-projective, we can moreover point to a particular GG-torsor E′→X′E^{\prime}\to X^{\prime} that is not a specialization of E→XE\to X and thus derive the quantitative Theorem 1.2.

Theorem 1.3 is not a corollary of Theorem 1.2, but its proof follows a simpler version of the above strategy. Loosely speaking, we make use of the torus contained in GG rather than the copy of 𝝁ℓ{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell}.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 recalls necessary facts about algebraic groups, torsors and vector bundles. Sections 3 and 4 are dedicated to proving Theorems 3.6 and 4.5, respectively. In Section 5, we give many examples of both torsion and non-torsion line bundles over smooth affine schemes requiring many global sections to generate, thus proving Theorem 5.1. These results are used in Section 6 to prove Theorems 1.1 and 1.2. Finally, Theorem 1.3 is proved in Section 7.

2. Preliminaries

Throughout this work, kk denotes a field and k¯\overline{k} is an algebraic closure of kk. If not indicated otherwise, all schemes and group schemes are over kk, morphisms are kk-morphisms, and products of schemes are taken over Spec⁡k\Spec k. By a kk-variety we mean an integral separated kk-scheme of finite type. The nn-dimensional affine and projective spaces over kk are denoted 𝔸n{\mathbb{A}}^{n} and ℙn{\mathbb{P}}^{n}, respectively.

A kk-ring means a commutative (unital) kk-algebra. A kk-field is a field extension of kk. If AA is a kk-ring and XX is a kk-scheme, we write XAX_{A} or X×kAX\times_{k}A for X×Spec⁡kSpec⁡AX\times_{\Spec k}\Spec A viewed as an AA-scheme. For example, ℙAn{\mathbb{P}}^{n}_{A} is the nn-dimensional projective space over Spec⁡A\Spec A. Similar notation applies to kk-morphisms.

A kk-group is a group scheme over kk. An algebraic kk-group or an algebraic group over kk means a kk-group of finite type (possibly non-smooth). Recall that an algebraic kk-group GG is affine if and only if it is linear. The identity connected component of GG is denoted G∘G^{\circ} and its unipotent radical is radu⁡(G)\rad_{u}(G). By a multiplicative algebraic group, we mean an algebraic group of multiplicative type.

As usual, 𝐆𝐚{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{a}} is the additive group of kk, 𝐆𝐦{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}} is the multiplicative group of kk, 𝝁ℓ{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell} is the algebraic kk-group of ℓ\ell-th roots of unity, 𝐆𝐋n{\mathbf{GL}}_{n} is the algebraic kk-group of invertible n×nn\times n matrices and 𝐒𝐋n{\mathbf{SL}}_{n} is the algebraic kk-group of n×nn\times n matrices of determinant 11. When p=char⁡k>0p=\Char k>0, we also write 𝜶pr{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{p^{r}} for the subgroup of 𝐆𝐚{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{a}} cut by the equation xpr=0x^{p^{r}}=0. In accordance with our earlier conventions, given a kk-field KK, we write 𝐆𝐚,K{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{a},{K}} for the algebraic KK-group 𝐆𝐚×kK{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{a}}\times_{k}K, and likewise for 𝐆𝐦{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}, 𝝁ℓ{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell}, etcetera.

We shall sometimes view kk-schemes as sheaves on the site of all kk-schemes with the fppf topology, denoted (𝖲𝖼𝗁/k)fppf({\mathsf{Sch}}/k)_{\mathrm{fppf}}. In particular, kk-morphisms f:X→Yf:X\to Y will sometimes be defined by specifying their action on sections, namely, by specifying fS:X⁡(S)→Y⁡(S)f_{S}:X(S)\to Y(S) for every scheme SS. When GG is a kk-group acting on a kk-scheme XX, we will write X/GX/G to denote the sheafification of the presheaf S↦X⁡(S)/G⁡(S)S\mapsto X(S)/G(S) on (𝖲𝖼𝗁/k)fppf({\mathsf{Sch}}/k)_{\mathrm{fppf}}. We shall treat X/GX/G as a kk-scheme when it is represented by one. For example, if GG is a subgroup of an algebraic kk-group HH, then H/GH/G is known to be a kk-scheme, which is moreover quasi-projective when HH is affine [23, Thm. 5.28, §7e, proof of Thm. 7.18].

Let GG be a kk-group scheme. Our conventions regarding GG-torsors are the same as in [12, §1]. That is, a GG-torsor over a kk-scheme XX consists of a sheaf EE on (𝖲𝖼𝗁/k)fppf({\mathsf{Sch}}/k)_{\mathrm{fppf}} together with a morphism E→XE\to X and a right GG-action E×G→EE\times G\to E subject to the requirement that there is an fppf covering X′→XX^{\prime}\to X for which X′×XE≅X′×kGX^{\prime}\times_{X}E\cong X^{\prime}\times_{k}G as schemes over X′X^{\prime} carrying a GG-action. Thus, GG-torsors over XX are classified by the cohomology pointed set Hfppf1​(X,G){\mathrm{H}}^{1}_{\mathrm{fppf}}(X,G). In general, not all GG-torsors are represented by a kk-scheme, but this is true if GG is affine [24, III, Thm. 4.3].

Let E→XE\to X be a GG-torsor and let f:Y→Xf:Y\to X be a morphism. Then the first projection Y×XE→YY\times_{X}E\to Y is also a GG-torsor; we write f∗​Ef^{*}E for Y×XEY\times_{X}E. We say that a GG-torsor E→XE\to X specializes to another GG-torsor E′→X′E^{\prime}\to X^{\prime} if there is a kk-morphism f:X′→Xf:X^{\prime}\to X such that E′≅f∗​EE^{\prime}\cong f^{*}E as GG-torsors over YY. This is equivalent to the existence of a GG-equivariant map f^:E′→E\hat{f}:E^{\prime}\to E.

Given a morphism of kk-groups φ:G→H\varphi:G\to H and a GG-torsor p:E→Xp:E\to X, one can form the HH-torsor

φ∗​(p):E×GH→X.\varphi_{*}(p):E\times^{G}H\to X.

Here, E×GHE\times^{G}H is the quotient of E×kHE\times_{k}H by the equivalence relation

(e,g,h)↦((e​g,h),(e,φ⁡(g)​h)):E×G×H→(E×H)×(E×H),(e,g,h)\mapsto((eg,h),(e,\varphi(g)h)):E\times G\times H\to(E\times H)\times(E\times H),

and φ∗​(p)\varphi_{*}(p) is given by φ∗​(p)​[e,h]=p⁡(e)\varphi_{*}(p)[e,h]=p(e) on sections.

A vector bundle over a kk-scheme XX is a locally free 𝒪X{\mathcal{O}}_{X}-module VV. In this case, the functor (f:Y→X)↦Γ(Y,f∗V)(f:Y\to X)\mapsto\Gamma(Y,f^{*}V) from XX-schemes to sets is represented by a scheme which we also denote by VV. (Here, as usual, f∗​V=f−1​V⊗f−1​𝒪X𝒪Yf^{*}V=f^{-1}V\otimes_{f^{-1}{\mathcal{O}}_{X}}{\mathcal{O}}_{Y}.)

Recall that there is a bijection between isomorphism classes of rank-nn vector bundles on XX and isomorphism classes of 𝐆𝐋n{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}-torsors over XX. Moreover, this equivalence is compatible with base-change. Briefly, given a rank-nn vector bundle VV, we can choose a Zariski covering {Ui→X}i∈I\{U_{i}\to X\}_{i\in I} and isomorphisms {φi:𝒪Uin→VUi}i∈I\{\varphi_{i}:{\mathcal{O}}_{U_{i}}^{n}\to V_{U_{i}}\}_{i\in I}. Setting Ui​j=Ui∩UjU_{ij}=U_{i}\cap U_{j}, this data gives rise to a 𝐆𝐋n{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}-valued 11-cocycle on XX, namely α={φj−1|Ui​j∘φi|Ui​j}i,j∈I\alpha=\{\varphi_{j}^{-1}|_{U_{ij}}\circ\varphi_{i}|_{U_{ij}}\}_{i,j\in I}, and it defines the 𝐆𝐋n{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}-torsor corresponding to VV (as well as its cohomology class in Hfppf1​(X,𝐆𝐋n){\mathrm{H}}^{1}_{\mathrm{fppf}}(X,{\mathbf{GL}}_{n})).

A line bundle LL over XX is a rank-11 vector bundle over XX. We say that LL is ℓ\ell-torsion (ℓ∈ℕ∪{0}\ell\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}) if L⊗ℓ:=L⊗𝒪X⋯⊗𝒪XLL^{\otimes\ell}:=L\otimes_{{\mathcal{O}}_{X}}\dots\otimes_{{\mathcal{O}}_{X}}L (ℓ\ell times) is isomorphic to 𝒪X{\mathcal{O}}_{X}. Note that every line bundle is 00-torsion. By the previous paragraph, there is a one-to-one correspondence between isomorphism classes of line bundles over XX, isomorphism classes of 𝐆𝐦{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}-torsors over XX and Hfppf1​(X,𝐆𝐦){\mathrm{H}}^{1}_{\mathrm{fppf}}(X,{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}). For ℓ>0\ell>0, the Kummer short exact sequence 𝝁ℓ↪𝐆𝐦→ℓ→𝐆𝐦{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell}\hookrightarrow{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}\xrightarrow{\ell}\mathrel{\mkern-14.0mu}\rightarrow{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}} of sheaves on (𝖲𝖼𝗁/k)fppf({\mathsf{Sch}}/k)_{\mathrm{fppf}} gives rise to a long cohomology exact sequence

…→Hfppf1​(X,𝝁ℓ)→Hfppf1​(X,𝐆𝐦)→ℓHfppf1​(X,𝐆𝐦)→…,\dots\to{\mathrm{H}}^{1}_{\mathrm{fppf}}(X,{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell})\to{\mathrm{H}}^{1}_{\mathrm{fppf}}(X,{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}})\xrightarrow{\ell}{\mathrm{H}}^{1}_{\mathrm{fppf}}(X,{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}})\to\dots,

from which we see that every 𝝁ℓ{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell}-torsor gives rise to an ℓ\ell-torsion line bundle, and every ℓ\ell-torsion line bundle arises from some 𝝁ℓ{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell}-torsor (that is not unique in general). Explicitly, the line bundle arising from a 𝝁ℓ{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell}-torsor T→XT\to X corresponds to the 𝐆𝐦{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}-torsor T×𝝁ℓ𝐆𝐦→XT\times^{{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell}}{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}\to X.

3. A Characterization of Non-Unipotent Groups

Recall the following important result: Among smooth connected linear algebraic groups over a field kk, unipotent groups are characterized by the property that they do not contain a nontrivial multiplicative subgroup. When kk is algebraically closed, this is [7, Ch. IV, Cor. 11.5(2)], and over general fields it follows from Grothendieck’s theorem on the existence of geometrically maximal tori (that is, tori defined over kk which are maximal over k¯\overline{k}) [9, Exp. XIV, Th. 1.1]. Our goal in this section is to prove an analogous result for all connected algebraic groups over general fields, and arbitrary algebraic groups over algebraically closed fields. The result for connected affine groups over algebraically closed fields is contained in SGA [9, Exp. XVII, Prop. 4.3.1, (i)⇔\iff(iv)]. In fact, the same proof works over perfect fields. The purpose of this section is to prove the same result without affineness or perfectness hypotheses.

We begin with the following lemma.

Lemma 3.1.

Over a field kk, an extension of a nontrivial finite connected multiplicative algebraic kk-group MM by a finite connected unipotent algebraic kk-group UU contains a nontrivial multiplicative algebraic kk-group.

Proof.

We may assume that char⁡(k)=p>0{\rm{char}}(k)=p>0 (otherwise MM is trivial), and that MM is pp-torsion [23, Cor. 11.30]. By [9, Exp. XVII, Prop. 4.2.1,(i)⇔\iff(iii)], we may also assume that U=𝜶prU={\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{p}^{r}. The proof is now essentially identical to that given in [23, Cor. 15.33], using [23, Prop. 15.31]. ∎

The key case, when GG is finite connected, is contained in the following lemma.

Lemma 3.2.

Let kk be a field of characteristic p>0p>0. A finite connected kk-group scheme II is unipotent if and only if it does not contain a nontrivial multiplicative subgroup.

Proof.

The “only if” direction is trivial, so we concentrate on the converse. First assume that II is commutative. The connected-étale sequence of I^\widehat{I}, the Cartier dual of II, then shows that I^\widehat{I} must be connected (since II does not contain a multiplicative group), hence II is a commutative infinitesimal (that is, finite connected) kk-group with infinitesimal dual. This implies that it is unipotent. (In fact, for this it is not hard to show that it is enough to have infinitesimal dual.) Indeed, by filtering we may suppose that II and its dual are both killed by Frobenius, and Dieudonné theory [8, Th. 1.4.3.2] then implies that, at least over the perfection of kk, II is isomorphic to a power of 𝜶p{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{p}, which then implies that it is unipotent; see [9, Exp. XVII, Def. 1.3].

We now prove the result in general by induction on the order of II. Note first that if one has an exact sequence

1⟶I′⟶I⟶I′′⟶11\longrightarrow I^{\prime}\longrightarrow I\longrightarrow I^{\prime\prime}\longrightarrow 1

with I′​⊴​II^{\prime}\trianglelefteq I proper and nontrivial, then by induction I′I^{\prime} is unipotent. If I′′I^{\prime\prime} contained a nontrivial multiplicative subgroup scheme, then so would II by Lemma 3.1. Therefore, I′′I^{\prime\prime} does not contain such a copy, so is also unipotent by induction, hence so is II. We are therefore free to assume that II does not admit a normal nontrivial proper kk-subgroup. In particular, we may assume that the Frobenius morphism of II is trivial. That is, II is a height one algebraic group.

Thanks to the equivalence between height one algebraic kk-groups and pp-Lie algebras [9, Exp. VIIA, Thm. 8.1.2], and the fact that we have already handled the commutative case, the problem translates into the following pp-Lie algebra question: If 𝔤\mathfrak{g} is a nonabelian pp-Lie algebra admitting no proper nonzero pp-ideals (that is, ideals preserved by the pp operation), then 𝔤\mathfrak{g} contains a nontrivial abelian pp-Lie subalgebra with surjective pp operation. Indeed, this follows from the fact that multiplicative groups have surjective pp operation (just check over an algebraic closure where it reduces to the case of 𝝁n{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{n}) while unipotent commutative groups of height one have nilpotent pp operation (as all such groups over an algebraic closure admit a filtration by either 𝜶p{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{p} or ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}), plus the fact that all commutative finite kk-groups may be filtered by multiplicative and unipotent ones.

First assume that ad⁡(X){\rm{ad}}(X) is nilpotent for all X∈𝔤X\in\mathfrak{g}. Then Engel’s theorem implies that 𝔤\mathfrak{g} is a nilpotent Lie algebra. In particular, it has nontrivial center. Since ad⁡(X[p])=ad​(X)p{\rm{ad}}(X^{[p]})={\rm{ad}}(X)^{p}, the center is preserved by the pp operation. It follows from our assumption that 𝔤\mathfrak{g} has no proper nonzero ideals that 𝔤\mathfrak{g} is abelian, contrary to assumption.

Now assume that not all ad⁡(X){\rm{ad}}(X) are nilpotent. Let X∈𝔤X\in\mathfrak{g} be such that ad⁡(X){\rm{ad}}(X) is not nilpotent. If f⁡(T)∈k⁡[T]f(T)\in k[T] is the minimal polynomial of ad⁡(X){\rm{ad}}(X), then ff is not a power of TT. Furthermore, for some r≥0r\geq 0, f⁡(T)=g⁡(Tpr)f(T)=g(T^{p^{r}}) with g∈k⁡[T]g\in k[T] separable. Because ad⁡(X[pr])=ad​(X)pr{\rm{ad}}(X^{[p^{r}]})={\rm{ad}}(X)^{p^{r}}, gg is the minimal polynomial of ad⁡(X[pr]){\rm{ad}}(X^{[p^{r}]}). Therefore, replacing XX by X[pr]X^{[p^{r}]}, we may assume that ad⁡(X){\rm{ad}}(X) is non-nilpotent and that its minimal polynomial is separable over kk. It follows that XX admits a Jordan-Chevalley decomposition X=Xs+XnX=X_{s}+X_{n} with ad⁡(Xs){\rm{ad}}(X_{s}) geometrically semisimple, and ad⁡(Xn){\rm{ad}}(X_{n}) nilpotent. Replacing XX by XsX_{s}, therefore, we obtain nonzero X∈𝔤X\in\mathfrak{g} such that ad⁡(X){\rm{ad}}(X) is geometrically semisimple.

Consider the nonzero subspace 𝔥:=⟨X,X[p],X[p2],…⟩⊂𝔤\mathfrak{h}:=\langle X,X^{[p]},X^{[p^{2}]},\dots\rangle\subset\mathfrak{g}. We claim that 𝔥\mathfrak{h} is abelian. Indeed, this follows from the fact that, for any Y∈𝔤Y\in\mathfrak{g}, ad⁡(Y[pn])=ad​(Y)pn{\rm{ad}}(Y^{[p^{n}]})={\rm{ad}}(Y)^{p^{n}}, hence Y[pn]Y^{[p^{n}]} commutes with YY. This equation also shows that ad⁡(Y)∈𝔤​𝔩​(𝔤){\rm{ad}}(Y)\in\mathfrak{gl}(\mathfrak{g}) is geometrically semisimple for all Y∈𝔥Y\in\mathfrak{h}. Because 𝔥\mathfrak{h} is abelian, one has (Y+Z)[p]=Y[p]+Z[p](Y+Z)^{[p]}=Y^{[p]}+Z^{[p]} for any Y,Z∈𝔥Y,Z\in\mathfrak{h}. Thus 𝔥⊂𝔤\mathfrak{h}\subset\mathfrak{g} is a (nonzero) abelian pp-Lie subalgebra of 𝔤\mathfrak{g} all of whose elements have geometrically semisimple adjoint action on 𝔤\mathfrak{g}, and furthermore this property is preserved upon passage to k¯\overline{k}.

We must show that the pp operation on 𝔥\mathfrak{h} is surjective, and it suffices to show this after extending scalars to k¯\overline{k}, where it is equivalent to injectivity, so we may assume that kk is algebraically closed. Suppose we are given Y∈𝔥Y\in\mathfrak{h} such that Y[p]=0Y^{[p]}=0. We must show that Y=0Y=0. One has ad⁡(Y[p])=ad​(Y)p=0∈𝔤​𝔩​(𝔤){\rm{ad}}(Y^{[p]})={\rm{ad}}(Y)^{p}=0\in\mathfrak{gl}(\mathfrak{g}). Because ad⁡(Y){\rm{ad}}(Y) is (geometrically) semisimple, it follows that ad⁡(Y)=0{\rm{ad}}(Y)=0. That is, YY is central in 𝔤\mathfrak{g}. Since Y[p]=0Y^{[p]}=0, it follows that ⟨Y⟩\langle Y\rangle is a pp-ideal of 𝔤\mathfrak{g}, a contradiction because we assumed that 𝔤\mathfrak{g} is nonabelian with no proper nonzero pp-ideals. This contradiction shows that the pp operation on 𝔥\mathfrak{h} is injective, and completes the proof of the lemma. ∎

Lemma 3.3.

Let kk be a perfect field. Then any extension EE of a multiplicative étale algebraic kk-group MM by a connected unipotent algebraic kk-group UU splits.

Proof.

By [9, Exp. XVII, Prop. 4.3.1(i)⇔\iff(iii)], we may assume that UU is a power of either 𝐆a\mathbf{G}_{a} or 𝜶p{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{p}. The former case follows from [23, Prop. 15.31], while the latter follows from [9, Exp. XVII, Lem. 1.6]. ∎

The following two lemmas will be required in order to deal with groups that are not affine. The non-affine case will not be needed in the next sections.

Lemma 3.4.

If GG is a connected algebraic group over a field kk, then there is an exact sequence of algebraic groups over kk

1⟶H⟶G⟶A⟶11\longrightarrow H\longrightarrow G\longrightarrow A\longrightarrow 1

with HH affine and connected and AA an abelian variety.

Proof.

By [9, Exp. VIIA, Prop. 8.3], there is an infinitesimal normal algebraic kk-group I​⊴​GI\trianglelefteq G such that G/IG/I is smooth, so we are free to assume that GG is smooth. If kk is perfect, then we are done by Chevalley’s Theorem. Otherwise, GkperfG_{k_{{\rm{perf}}}} may be written as an extension of an abelian variety by a linear algebraic kk-group, and therefore Gkp−nG_{k^{p^{-n}}} may be so written for some n≥0n\geq 0. Via the isomorphism kp−n→∼kk^{p^{-n}}\xrightarrow{\sim}k, λ↦λpn\lambda\mapsto\lambda^{p^{n}}, Gkp−nG_{k^{p^{-n}}} is identified with G(pn)G^{(p^{n})}, the nn-fold Frobenius twist of GG. Therefore, G(pn)G^{(p^{n})} may be written as an extension of an abelian variety by a linear algebraic group. Since GG is smooth, the nn-fold Frobenius map G→G(pn)G\rightarrow G^{(p^{n})} is surjective, hence the result for GG. ∎

Lemma 3.5.

Over a field kk of characteristic p>0p>0, for any extension EE of an abelian variety AA by a unipotent algebraic kk-group UU, there is an integer n≥0n\geq 0 such that the extension splits upon pullback by the map [pn]:A→A[p^{n}]\colon A\rightarrow A.

Proof.

We may assume that UU is either connected or finite étale. In the latter case, we may by filtration assume that UU is commutative and pp-torsion. In the former case, [9, Exp. XVII, Prop. 4.3.1(i)⇔\iff(iii)] allows us to assume that UU is a power of either 𝜶p{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{p} or 𝐆𝐚{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{a}}. Thus we may assume that UU is either pp-torsion finite étale commutative, or else a power of either 𝜶p{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{p} or 𝐆𝐚{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{a}}. If the extension EE is commutative, then because UU is pp-torsion, Ext1⁡(A,U)\Ext^{1}(A,U) is killed by [p][p], hence [p]A[p]_{A} induces the 00 map on Ext1⁡(A,U)\Ext^{1}(A,U), which proves the lemma. It therefore only remains to prove that EE is commutative.

First suppose that UU is either finite étale or a power of 𝜶p{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{p}. Then the automorphism functor AutU/k{\rm{Aut}}_{U/k} of UU is an affine kk-group scheme, and the conjugation action of AA on UU is then given by a homomorphism A→AutU/kA\rightarrow{\rm{Aut}}_{U/k}, which must be trivial. Therefore, EE is a central extension. The commutator map of EE therefore descends to a map A×A→UA\times A\rightarrow U, which must be constant because UU is finite and A×AA\times A is connected and geometrically reduced. Thus EE is commutative.

It remains to show that EE is commutative under the assumption that U=𝐆𝐚rU={\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{a}}^{r} for some r>0r>0. Once again, conjugation induces an action of AA on 𝐆𝐚r{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{a}}^{r}. But we claim that any such action is trivial, and hence EE is central. To prove this, we may temporarily extend scalars and thereby assume that kk is infinite. Then for any x∈kr=𝐆𝐚r​(k)x\in k^{r}={\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{a}}^{r}(k), the map a↦a⋅xa\mapsto a\cdot x induces a map A→𝐆𝐚rA\rightarrow{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{a}}^{r}. Because 𝐆𝐚r{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{a}}^{r} is affine, this map must be constant, hence AA acts trivially on xx. Because 𝐆𝐚r​(k){\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{a}}^{r}(k) is Zariski dense in 𝐆𝐚r{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{a}}^{r}, it follows that the action of AA on 𝐆𝐚r{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{a}}^{r} is trivial and EE is central, as claimed. Once again, therefore, the commutator map of EE descends to a map A×A→𝐆𝐚rA\times A\rightarrow{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{a}}^{r} which must be constant because the target is affine. Thus EE is commutative, and the proof is complete. ∎

We now prove the main result of this section.

Theorem 3.6.

Let kk be a field and GG an algebraic group over kk.

  • (i)

    If GG is connected, then GG is unipotent if and only if it does not contain a nontrivial multiplicative algebraic kk-group.

  • (ii)

    If kk is algebraically closed, then GG is unipotent if and only if it does not contain a nontrivial multiplicative algebraic kk-group.

Proof.

The “only if” direction is immediate, so we concentrate on the “if” direction. First we prove (i). Let GG be a connected algebraic group over kk that has no nontrivial multiplicative subgroup. We must show that GG is unipotent. Let us first give the proof under the additional assumption that GG is affine. By [9, Exp. VIIA, Prop. 8.3], there is an infinitesimal (i.e., finite connected) algebraic subgroup I​⊴​GI\trianglelefteq G such that G¯:=G/I\overline{G}:=G/I is smooth (and connected), and II is unipotent by Lemma 3.2. If G¯\overline{G} contains a nontrivial kk-torus, then Lemma 3.1 implies that GG contains a nontrivial multiplicative subgroup. Therefore, G¯\overline{G} does not contain a nontrivial torus, hence is unipotent by [7, Ch. IV, Cor. 11.5(2)] and [9, Exp. XIV, Thm. 1.1], which completes the proof in the affine case.

In the general (not necessarily affine) case, Lemma 3.4 furnishes an exact sequence

1⟶H⟶G⟶A⟶11\longrightarrow H\longrightarrow G\longrightarrow A\longrightarrow 1

with HH connected and affine, and AA an abelian variety. By the already-treated affine case, HH is unipotent. Assume for the sake of contradiction that A≠0A\neq 0. First suppose that char⁡k=0\Char k=0, or even just that kk is perfect. For any n>1n>1 not divisible by char⁡k\Char k, A⁡[n]A[n] is a nontrivial étale multiplicative algebraic group [40, Tag 03RP], hence Lemma 3.3 implies that GG contains such an algebraic group, in violation of our assumption.

Now suppose that char⁡k=p>0\Char k=p>0. By Lemma 3.5, GG contains a copy of AA. If AA were nontrivial, it would follow that GG contains a nontrivial multiplicative subgroup — for instance, A⁡[n]A[n] for any n>1n>1 not divisible by char⁡k\Char k. It follows that A=0A=0.

For (ii), let GG be an algebraic group over kk not containing a nontrivial multiplicative subgroup. By (i), G0G^{0} is unipotent, and we need only show that the finite constant algebraic kk-group E:=G/G0E:=G/G^{0} is unipotent – that is, E⁡(k)E(k) is a pp-group. If not, then E⁡(k)E(k) admits a nontrivial nn-torsion element for some nn not divisible by pp. This element then defines a nontrivial multiplicative étale kk-subgroup of EE, so GG contains such a group by Lemma 3.3. This violates our assumption about GG, hence completes the proof. ∎

Remark 3.7.

The assumption of connectedness in Theorem 3.6(i) is necessary beyond the algebraically closed case. Indeed, for kk imperfect of characteristic pp, for instance, [23, Cor. 15.33] implies that there are non-split extensions of 𝝁ℓ{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell} by 𝜶p{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}_{p} for primes ℓ≠p\ell\neq p. Such an extension is not unipotent, but it cannot contain a nontrivial multiplicative subgroup, as this would yield a splitting of the extension.

4. Reduction to a Statement About Torsion Line Bundles

Let kk be a field and let GG be a linear algebraic group over kk. The purpose of this section is to show that if a GG-torsor E→XE\to X is weakly versal for a class of affine kk-schemes 𝒞{\mathscr{C}} and GG contains a copy of 𝝁ℓ{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell} (resp. 𝐆𝐦{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}), then there is a uniform upper bound on the number of generators of an ℓ\ell-torsion (resp. any) line-bundle over a scheme in 𝒞{\mathscr{C}}. This is stated formally in Theorem 4.5 which makes use of the following invariant.

Definition 4.1.

Let VV be a vector bundle of rank nn over a scheme XX. An open covering 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} of XX is said to split VV if VU≅𝒪UnV_{U}\cong{\mathcal{O}}_{U}^{n} for all U∈𝒰U\in{\mathcal{U}}. The smallest possible cardinality of a covering which splits VV is called the splitting number of VV and denoted

spl⁡(V).\spl(V).

Observe that spl⁡(V)\spl(V) is finite if XX is quasi-compact. Furthermore, for every morphism f:Y→Xf:Y\to X, we have spl⁡(f∗​V)≤spl⁡(V)\spl(f^{*}V)\leq\spl(V).

Proposition 4.2.

Let XX be a noetherian scheme such that every finite collection of closed points of XX is contained in an open affine subscheme of XX, e.g., a quasi-projective scheme over a field. Let VV be a rank-nn vector bundle over XX. Then spl⁡(V)≤dimX+1\spl(V)\leq\dim X+1.

Proof.

It is enough to show that there is a sequence {Ui}i=1dimX+1\{U_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\dim X+1} of open affine subsets of XX such that VUr≅𝒪UrnV_{U_{r}}\cong{\mathcal{O}}_{U_{r}}^{n} and dim(X−⋃i=1rUi)≤dimX−r\dim(X-\bigcup_{i=1}^{r}U_{i})\leq\dim X-r for all r∈{0,1,…,dimX+1}r\in\{0,1,\dots,\dim X+1\}. Indeed, if this holds, then {Ui}i=1dimX+1\{U_{i}\}_{i=1}^{\dim X+1} is a covering of XX which splits VV. We prove the existence of the sequence by induction. Let r∈{1,…,dimX+1}r\in\{1,\dots,\dim X+1\} and suppose that U1,…,Ur−1U_{1},\dots,U_{r-1} were constructed. Put Y=X−⋃i=1r−1UiY=X-\bigcup_{i=1}^{r-1}U_{i} and let y1,…,yty_{1},\dots,y_{t} be closed points of YY meeting every irreducible component of YY. These points are also closed in XX, so there is an open affine U⊆XU\subseteq X with y1,…,yt∈Uy_{1},\dots,y_{t}\in U. Since UU is affine, the semilocalization of VUV_{U} at {y1,…,yt}\{y_{1},\dots,y_{t}\} is free. We may therefore shrink UU to assume that VU≅𝒪UnV_{U}\cong{\mathcal{O}}_{U}^{n}. Now take UrU_{r} to be UU. We have VUr≅𝒪UrnV_{U_{r}}\cong{\mathcal{O}}_{U_{r}}^{n} by construction, and since UrU_{r} meets every irreducible component of YY, we also have dim(X−⋃i=1rUi)=dim(Y−Ur)≤dimY−1≤dimX−(r−1)−1=dimX−r\dim(X-\bigcup_{i=1}^{r}U_{i})=\dim(Y-U_{r})\leq\dim Y-1\leq\dim X-(r-1)-1=\dim X-r. ∎

Let XX be a scheme, let ℳ{\mathcal{M}} be an 𝒪X{\mathcal{O}}_{X}-module and let S⊆Γ⁡(X,ℳ)S\subseteq\Gamma(X,{\mathcal{M}}). As usual, we say that SS generates ℳ{\mathcal{M}} if the 𝒪X{\mathcal{O}}_{X}-module map

(αs)s∈S↦∑s∈Sαs​s:⨁S𝒪X→ℳ(\alpha_{s})_{s\in S}\mapsto\sum_{s\in S}\alpha_{s}s:\bigoplus_{S}{\mathcal{O}}_{X}\to{\mathcal{M}}

is surjective. The 𝒪X{\mathcal{O}}_{X}-module ℳ{\mathcal{M}} is said to be globally generated if there is some S⊆Γ⁡(X,ℳ)S\subseteq\Gamma(X,{\mathcal{M}}) generating ℳ{\mathcal{M}}, and in this case we write

gen⁡(ℳ)\gen({\mathcal{M}})

for the minimal possible cardinality of such SS. This number is always finite if XX is affine and ℳ{\mathcal{M}} is quasicoherent of finite type.

Proposition 4.3.

Let XX be an affine scheme and let VV be a rank-nn vector bundle over XX. Then gen⁡(V)≤n​spl⁡(V)\gen(V)\leq n\spl(V).

Proof.

Write r=spl⁡(V)r=\spl(V). Then XX has an open covering {U1,…,Ur}\{U_{1},\dots,U_{r}\} splitting VV. Write X=Spec⁡AX=\Spec A. Then there are ideals I1,…,Ir⊴AI_{1},\dots,I_{r}\unlhd A such that

Ui={𝔭∈Spec⁡A:Ii⊈𝔭}U_{i}=\{{\mathfrak{p}}\in\Spec A\,:\,I_{i}\nsubseteq{\mathfrak{p}}\}

for every i∈{1,…,r}i\in\{1,\dots,r\}. Since X=⋃i=1rUiX=\bigcup_{i=1}^{r}U_{i}, we have ∑i=1rIi=A\sum_{i=1}^{r}I_{i}=A. Thus, we can choose ai∈Iia_{i}\in I_{i} for every ii such that ∑i=1rai=1A\sum_{i=1}^{r}a_{i}=1_{A}. Let WiW_{i} be the principal open affine corresponding to aia_{i}, namely,

Wi={𝔭∈Spec⁡A:ai∉𝔭}.W_{i}=\{{\mathfrak{p}}\in\Spec A\,:\,a_{i}\notin{\mathfrak{p}}\}.

Then X=⋃i=1rWiX=\bigcup_{i=1}^{r}W_{i} and Wi⊆UiW_{i}\subseteq U_{i} for all ii.

Let i∈{1,…,r}i\in\{1,\dots,r\}. Since VUi≅𝒪UinV_{U_{i}}\cong{\mathcal{O}}_{U_{i}}^{n}, we also have VWi≅𝒪WinV_{W_{i}}\cong{\mathcal{O}}_{W_{i}}^{n}. Thus, there exist f1(i),…,fn(i)∈Γ⁡(Wi,V)f_{1}^{(i)},\dots,f_{n}^{(i)}\in\Gamma(W_{i},V) that generate VWiV_{W_{i}}. By construction, Γ⁡(Wi,V)\Gamma(W_{i},V) is the localization of the AA-module Γ⁡(X,V)\Gamma(X,V) at the multiplicative set {1,ai,ai2,…}\{1,a_{i},a_{i}^{2},\dots\}, so there are g1(i),…,gn(i)∈Γ⁡(X,V)g_{1}^{(i)},\dots,g_{n}^{(i)}\in\Gamma(X,V) and k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} such that fj(i)=ai−k​gj(i)f_{j}^{(i)}=a_{i}^{-k}g_{j}^{(i)} for all j∈{1,…,n}j\in\{1,\dots,n\}.

Finally, put S={gj(i)|i∈{1,…,r},j∈{1,…,n}}S=\{g^{(i)}_{j}\,|\,i\in\{1,\dots,r\},j\in\{1,\dots,n\}\}. Then every x∈Xx\in X admits an open neighborhood where SS generates VV. Since generating VV is a Zariski-local property, this means that SS generates VV, and it follows that gen⁡(V)≤|S|≤n​r\gen(V)\leq|S|\leq nr. ∎

We now prove a key lemma.

Lemma 4.4.

Let kk be a field and let ℓ\ell be a prime number. Let MM be 𝐆𝐦{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}} or 𝛍ℓ{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell}, let ρ:M→𝐆𝐋n\rho:M\to{\mathbf{GL}}_{n} be a monomorphism of algebraic kk-groups, and let {x↦xai}i=1n\{x\mapsto x^{a_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{n} denote the characters of MM occurring in the representation ρ\rho. Let E→XE\to X be a 𝐆𝐋n{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}-torsor corresponding to a rank-nn vector bundle VV, and let F→YF\to Y be an MM-torsor inducing a line bundle LL. Suppose further that YY is affine and E→XE\to X specializes to F×M𝐆𝐋n→YF\times^{M}{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}\to Y. Then:

  1. (i)

    When M=𝝁ℓM={\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell}, we have gen⁡(L)≤n​spl⁡(V)\gen(L)\leq n\spl(V).

  2. (ii)

    When M=𝐆𝐦M={\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}, we have gen⁡(L)≤(n​spl⁡(V))r\gen(L)\leq(n\spl(V))^{r}, where rr is the minimum of |S||S| as SS ranges over all nonempty subsets of {a1,…,an}\{a_{1},\dots,a_{n}\} with gcd⁡(S)=1\gcd(S)=1.

Proof.

We prove (i) and (ii) together. Write T=F×M𝐆𝐋nT=F\times^{M}{\mathbf{GL}}_{n} and denote by WW the rank-nn vector bundle over YY corresponding to TT.

Since MM is diagonalizable, we may replace ρ\rho with Int⁡(g)∘ρ\Int(g)\circ\rho for some g∈GLn​(k)g\in\mathrm{GL}_{n}({k}) to assume that ρ\rho is given section-wise by

φ⁡(x)=[xa1⋱xan].\varphi(x)=\begin{bmatrix}x^{a_{1}}&&\\ &\ddots&\\ &&x^{a_{n}}\end{bmatrix}.

This does not affect the isomorphism class of the 𝐆𝐋n{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}-torsor T→YT\to Y.

By assumption, there is a kk-morphism f:Y→Xf:Y\to X such that f∗​E≅Tf^{*}E\cong T as 𝐆𝐋n{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}-torsors. As a result, f∗​V≅Wf^{*}V\cong W and so spl⁡(W)≤spl⁡(V)\spl(W)\leq\spl(V). Since YY is affine, we may apply Proposition 4.3 to WW and get

gen⁡(W)≤n​spl⁡(V).\gen(W)\leq n\spl(V).

Next, observe that since T=M×𝝁ℓ𝐆𝐋nT=M\times^{{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell}}{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}, we have

W≅L⊗a1⊕⋯⊕L⊗an,W\cong L^{\otimes a_{1}}\oplus\dots\oplus L^{\otimes a_{n}},

where here, L⊗aL^{\otimes a} means (L∨)⊗(−a)(L^{\vee})^{\otimes(-a)} if a<0a<0. This can be seen by inspecting the cocycles representing the classes in Hfppf1​(Y,𝐆𝐋n){\mathrm{H}}^{1}_{\mathrm{fppf}}(Y,{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}) corresponding to both vector bundles. It follows that each L⊗aiL^{\otimes a_{i}} is an epimorphic image of WW, and therefore gen⁡(L⊗ai)≤gen⁡(W)≤n​spl⁡(V)\gen(L^{\otimes a_{i}})\leq\gen(W)\leq n\spl(V). By a lemma of Swan [6, Lem. 3.4], we moreover have gen⁡((L⊗ai)⊗b)≤gen⁡(L⊗ai)≤n​spl⁡(V)\gen((L^{\otimes a_{i}})^{\otimes b})\leq\gen(L^{\otimes a_{i}})\leq n\spl(V) for all b∈ℤb\in\mathbb{Z}.

Suppose now that H=𝝁ℓH={\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell}. Since ρ\rho is a monomorphism, there is some 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n with ℓ∤ai\ell\nmid a_{i}. Thus, there is b∈ℤb\in\mathbb{Z} such that ai​b≡1​(mod⁡ℓ)a_{i}b\equiv 1\,(\operatorname{mod}\ell). For that bb, we get gen⁡(L)=gen⁡((L⊗ai)⊗b)≤n​spl⁡(V)\gen(L)=\gen((L^{\otimes a_{i}})^{\otimes b})\leq n\spl(V), as required.

Finally, suppose that H=𝐆𝐦H={\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}. Since ρ\rho is a monomorphism, gcd⁡(a1,…,an)=1\gcd(a_{1},\dots,a_{n})=1. Choose a subset S⊆{a1,…,an}S\subseteq\{a_{1},\dots,a_{n}\} of cardinality rr such that gcd⁡(S)=1\gcd(S)=1, say S={ai1,…,air}S=\{a_{i_{1}},\dots,a_{i_{r}}\}. Then there are b1,…,br∈ℤb_{1},\dots,b_{r}\in\mathbb{Z} such that ∑j=1raij​bj=1\sum_{j=1}^{r}a_{i_{j}}b_{j}=1. Then L≅⨂j=1r(L⊗aij)⊗bjL\cong\bigotimes_{j=1}^{r}(L^{\otimes a_{i_{j}}})^{\otimes b_{j}}, and by what we have shown, gen⁡(L)≤∏i=1rgen⁡((L⊗aij)⊗bj)≤(n​spl⁡(V))r\gen(L)\leq\prod_{i=1}^{r}\gen((L^{\otimes a_{i_{j}}})^{\otimes b_{j}})\leq(n\spl(V))^{r}. ∎

Theorem 4.5.

Let kk be a field and let GG be a closed subgroup of 𝐆𝐋n{\mathbf{GL}}_{n} (n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}). Let E→XE\to X be a GG-torsor, and let VV denote the rank-nn vector bundle corresponding to E×G𝐆𝐋nE\times^{G}{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}. Suppose that E→XE\to X is versal for a class of affine kk-schemes 𝒞{\mathscr{C}}.

  1. (i)

    If GG contains a copy of 𝝁ℓ{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell} for some prime number ℓ\ell, then for every Y∈𝒞Y\in{\mathscr{C}} and every ℓ\ell-torsion line bundle LL on YY, we have gen⁡(L)≤n​spl⁡(V)\gen(L)\leq n\spl(V).

  2. (ii)

    If GG contains a copy of 𝐆𝐦{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}, then for every Y∈𝒞Y\in{\mathscr{C}} and every line bundle LL on YY, we have gen⁡(L)≤(n​spl⁡(V))r\gen(L)\leq(n\spl(V))^{r}, where rr is the number in Lemma 4.4(ii) attached to the monomorphism 𝐆𝐦→G→𝐆𝐋n{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}\to G\to{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}.

Proof.

(i) Let Y∈𝒞Y\in{\mathscr{C}} and let LL be an ℓ\ell-torsion line bundle on YY. Choose a 𝝁ℓ{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell}-torsor F→YF\to Y inducing YY. Since the GG-torsor E→XE\to X is weakly versal for 𝒞{\mathscr{C}}, it specializes to F×𝝁ℓGF\times^{{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell}}G. This means that the 𝐆𝐋n{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}-torsor F×𝝁ℓ𝐆𝐋n=(F×𝝁ℓG)×G​𝐆𝐋nF\times^{{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell}}{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}=(F\times^{{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell}}G)^{\times G}{\mathbf{GL}}_{n} (over YY) is a specialization of E×G𝐆𝐋nE\times^{G}{\mathbf{GL}}_{n} (over XX). Applying Lemma 4.4(i) to E×G𝐆𝐋n→XE\times^{G}{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}\to X now gives the desired conclusion gen⁡(L)≤n​spl⁡(V)\gen(L)\leq n\spl(V).

(ii) The proof is the same as in (i) except we use Lemma 4.4(ii). ∎

5. Torsion Line Bundles Requiring Many Sections to Generate

Let kk be a field. The purpose of this section is to show that for every m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N} and 1<ℓ∈ℕ1<\ell\in\mathbb{N}, there is an ℓ\ell-torsion line bundle over a smooth affine kk-scheme XX that requires at least mm global sections to generate. This will be coupled with Theorem 4.5 in the next section in order to prove Theorem 1.1.

For any m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}, the existence of affine schemes of finite type over ℝ\mathbb{R} admitting 22-torsion line bundles which cannot be generated by mm elements goes back at least as far as Swan [42, Thm. 4], who attributes the example to Chase. Similar 22-torsion examples over affine varieties over any field of characteristic not 22 were given by Shukla and Williams [38, Props. 7.13, 6.3].

Since the dimension of the base scheme XX would affect the quantitative version of Theorem 1.1, i.e. Theorem 1.2, we would like dimX\dim X to be as small as possible. To that end, given ℓ,m∈ℕ∪{0}\ell,m\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\} with ℓ≠1\ell\neq 1, it is convenient to define

gk​(ℓ,m)g_{k}(\ell,m)

to be the smallest d∈ℕ∪{0}d\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\} for which there exists a dd-dimensional smooth affine kk-scheme XX carrying an ℓ\ell-torsion line bundle LL satisfying gen⁡(L)>m\gen(L)>m. Note that gk​(0,m)g_{k}(0,m) is the minimal dimension of a smooth affine kk-scheme carrying a (possibly non-torsion) line bundle which cannot be generated by mm elements. By the end of this section, we will show:

Theorem 5.1.

Let kk be a field and let ℓ,m\ell,m be non-negative integers with ℓ≠1\ell\neq 1.

  1. (i)

    gk​(ℓ,0)=0g_{k}(\ell,0)=0 and gk​(ℓ,1)=1g_{k}(\ell,1)=1.

  2. (ii)

    gk​(ℓ,m)∈{m,m+1,m+2}g_{k}(\ell,m)\in\{m,m+1,m+2\}.

  3. (iii)

    If ℓ\ell is divisible by a prime number greater than mm (e.g. ℓ=0\ell=0), then gk​(ℓ,m)∈{m,m+1}g_{k}(\ell,m)\in\{m,m+1\}.

  4. (iv)

    If kk is algebraically closed, m>1m>1 and ℓ>0\ell>0, then gk​(ℓ,m)≥m+1g_{k}(\ell,m)\geq m+1. Equality holds if ℓ\ell is moreover divisible by a prime number greater than mm.

  5. (v)

    If char⁡k=0\Char k=0 and trdegℚ​k\mathrm{trdeg}_{\mathbb{Q}}k is infinite, then gk​(0,m)=mg_{k}(0,m)=m.

  6. (vi)

    g𝔽¯p​(0,m)=m+1g_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}(0,m)=m+1 for every prime p>0p>0 and m≥2m\geq 2.

We expect that part (v) also holds in positive characteristic, see Remark 5.16. The characteristic-00 counterpart of (vi), i.e., the statement gℚ¯​(0,m)=m+1g_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(0,m)=m+1, is related to the Bloch–Beilinson conjecture, and in particular follows from it (Remark 5.18). We do not know if there are kk, ℓ\ell, mm with gk​(ℓ,m)=m+2g_{k}(\ell,m)=m+2; this is related to conjectures of Paulsen and Griffiths–Harris (Remark 5.14).

In general, for ℓ>1\ell>1, the precise value of gk​(ℓ,m)g_{k}(\ell,m) is sensitive to arithmetic properties of the field kk. This demonstrated in Example 5.9 and Corollary 5.11.

We begin by recalling a result of Forster [17] (see [13] for a more modern treatment): Every rank-nn projective module over a noetherian ring of Krull dimension mm is generated by m+nm+n elements. This implies:

Lemma 5.2.

For every field kk and ℓ,m∈ℕ∪{0}\ell,m\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\} with ℓ≠1\ell\neq 1, we have gk​(ℓ,m)≥mg_{k}(\ell,m)\geq m.

In what follows, given a smooth (irreducible) kk-variety XX, we denote by CHi⁡X\CH^{i}X the ii-th Chow group of XX; see [18, §8.3]. The Chow ring of XX is CH∗⁡X=⨁i≥0CHi⁡X\CH^{*}X=\bigoplus_{i\geq 0}\CH^{i}X. Recall that a morphism f:X→Yf:X\to Y between smooth kk-varieties induces a ring homomorphism f∗:CH∗⁡Y→CH∗⁡Xf^{*}:\CH^{*}Y\to\CH^{*}X. If EE is a vector bundle over XX, then the ii-th Chern class of EE is denoted ci​(E)∈CHi⁡Xc_{i}(E)\in\CH^{i}X. The total Chern class of EE is c⁡(E)=∑i=0rank⁡Eci​(E)∈CH∗⁡Xc(E)=\sum_{i=0}^{\rank E}c_{i}(E)\in\CH^{*}X; see [18, §3.2] for details.

Proposition 5.3 (Murthy [27, Cor. 3.16]).

Suppose that kk is algebraically closed, let XX be a smooth affine kk-variety of dimension mm and let LL be a line bundle over XX. Then gen⁡(L)≤m\gen(L)\leq m if and only if c1​(L)m=0c_{1}(L)^{m}=0.

It turns out that the “only if” part of Murthy’s result holds for any smooth scheme over any field; this will be our main tool for bounding gk​(ℓ,m)g_{k}(\ell,m) from above.

Lemma 5.4.

Let XX be a smooth kk-variety, let LL be a line bundle over XX and let m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}. Suppose that c1​(L)m≠0c_{1}(L)^{m}\neq 0 in CHm⁡X\CH^{m}X. Then gen⁡(L)>m\gen(L)>m.

Proof.

For the sake of contradiction, suppose that LL can be generated by mm global sections. Then there is an exact sequence of vector bundles on XX,

0→E→𝒪X⊕m→L→0.0\to E\to{\mathcal{O}}_{X}^{\oplus m}\to L\to 0.

By tensoring with L∨L^{\vee}, the dual of LL, we get an exact sequence

0→E′→(L∨)⊕m→𝒪X→0,0\to E^{\prime}\to(L^{\vee})^{\oplus m}\to{\mathcal{O}}_{X}\to 0,

where E′=E⊗L∨E^{\prime}=E\otimes L^{\vee}. Thus,

c​(L∨)m=c⁡((L∨)⊕m)=c⁡(E′)​c​(𝒪X)=c⁡(E′).c(L^{\vee})^{m}=c((L^{\vee})^{\oplus m})=c(E^{\prime})c({\mathcal{O}}_{X})=c(E^{\prime}).

Since rank⁡E′=m−1\rank E^{\prime}=m-1, it follows that

(−1)m​c1​(L)m=c1​(L∨)m=cm​(E′)=0(-1)^{m}c_{1}(L)^{m}=c_{1}(L^{\vee})^{m}=c_{m}(E^{\prime})=0

in CHm⁡X\CH^{m}X. But this contradicts our assumptions. ∎

In light of Proposition 5.3 and Lemma 5.4, it is convenient to define

Gk​(ℓ,m)G_{k}(\ell,m)

to be the minimum possible dimension of a smooth affine kk-scheme XX admitting an ℓ\ell-torsion line bundle LL satisfying c1​(L)m≠0c_{1}(L)^{m}\neq 0. It is clear that Gk​(ℓ,m)≥mG_{k}(\ell,m)\geq m, and Proposition 5.3 and Lemma 5.4 imply:

Corollary 5.5.

For every field kk and integers ℓ,m≥0\ell,m\geq 0 with ℓ≠1\ell\neq 1, we have

gk​(ℓ,m)≤Gk​(ℓ,m).g_{k}(\ell,m)\leq G_{k}(\ell,m).

Moreover, when kk is algebraically closed, gk​(ℓ,m)=mg_{k}(\ell,m)=m if and only if Gk​(ℓ,m)=mG_{k}(\ell,m)=m.

We can use the second assertion of Corollary 5.5 and another result of Murthy to get a better lower bound on gk​(ℓ,m)g_{k}(\ell,m).

Proposition 5.6.

If kk is algebraically closed, ℓ>0\ell>0 and m≥2m\geq 2, then Gk​(ℓ,m)≥m+1G_{k}(\ell,m)\geq m+1. Consequently, gk​(ℓ,m)≥m+1g_{k}(\ell,m)\geq m+1.

Proof.

Let LL be an ℓ\ell-torsion line bundle over a smooth affine mm-dimensional kk-scheme XX. Murthy [27, Thms. 2.11, 2.14] showed that CHm⁡X\CH^{m}X is torsion-free. Since c1​(L)c_{1}(L) is ℓ\ell-torsion, we must have c1​(L)m=0c_{1}(L)^{m}=0. ∎

In the next results, we establish upper bounds on Gk​(ℓ,m)G_{k}(\ell,m) by exhibiting smooth affine kk-varieties XX carrying an ℓ\ell-torsion line bundle LL such that c1​(L)m≠0c_{1}(L)^{m}\neq 0. We will use the following proposition to produce such examples. Recall that the index of a kk-scheme XX, denoted ind⁡X\ind X, is the greatest common divisor of {dimkK|K is a finite k-field with X⁡(K)≠∅}\{\dim_{k}K\,|\,\text{$K$ is a finite $k$-field with $X(K)\neq\emptyset$}\}.

Proposition 5.7.

Let m,ℓ∈ℕm,\ell\in\mathbb{N} and let ZZ be an integral hypersurface in ℙm{\mathbb{P}}^{m} having degree dd and index nn. Let X=ℙm−ZX={\mathbb{P}}^{m}-Z, let L=𝒪ℙm​(1)|XL={\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{m}}(1)|_{X}, let X′X^{\prime} be the complement of the zero section in the total space of 𝒪ℙm​(ℓ)|X{\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{m}}(\ell)|_{X}, let p:X′→Xp:X^{\prime}\to X be its structure morphism and let L′=p∗​LL^{\prime}=p^{*}L. Then:

  1. (i)

    XX is affine, L⊗d≅𝒪XL^{\otimes d}\cong{\mathcal{O}}_{X} and the order of c1​(L)mc_{1}(L)^{m} in the (additive) group CHm⁡X\CH^{m}X is nn. Consequently, c1​(L)m≠0c_{1}(L)^{m}\neq 0 if n>1n>1.

  2. (ii)

    X′X^{\prime} is affine, L′⊗ℓ≅𝒪X′L^{\prime\otimes\ell}\cong{\mathcal{O}}_{X^{\prime}} and the order of c1​(L′)mc_{1}(L^{\prime})^{m} in CHm⁡X′\CH^{m}X^{\prime} is gcd⁡(n,ℓ)\gcd(n,\ell). Consequently, c1​(L′)m≠0c_{1}(L^{\prime})^{m}\neq 0 if gcd⁡(n,ℓ)>1\gcd(n,\ell)>1.

Proof.

(i) The scheme XX is affine because it is the complement of an ample divisor in ℙm{\mathbb{P}}^{m}.

Recall [18, §8.4] that CH∗⁡ℙm=ℤ⁡[h|hm+1=0]\CH^{*}{\mathbb{P}}^{m}=\mathbb{Z}[h\,|\,h^{m+1}=0], where hh is the class of a hyperplane in ℙm{\mathbb{P}}^{m} and lives in degree 11. Write CHi⁡(Z)\CH_{i}(Z) for the group of ii-cycles on ZZ modulo rational equivalence (we have CHi⁡(Z)=CHm−1−i⁡Z\CH_{i}(Z)=\CH^{m-1-i}Z when ZZ is smooth). By [18, Prop. 1.8], there is an exact sequence

(1) CHi⁡(Z)→CHm−i⁡ℙm→CHm−i⁡X→0\CH_{i}(Z)\to\CH^{m-i}{\mathbb{P}}^{m}\to\CH^{m-i}X\to 0

in which the first map is pushforward along Z→ℙmZ\to{\mathbb{P}}^{m} and the second map is pullback along X→ℙmX\to{\mathbb{P}}^{m}. Let AiA_{i} denote the image of CHi⁡(Z)\CH_{i}(Z) in CHm−i⁡ℙm=ℤ​hm−i\CH^{m-i}{\mathbb{P}}^{m}=\mathbb{Z}h^{m-i}. We may and shall identify CHm−i⁡X\CH^{m-i}X with ℤ​hm−i/Ai\mathbb{Z}h^{m-i}/A_{i} using (1). For i=0i=0, this gives

CHm⁡X=ℤ​hm/A0=ℤ​hm/ℤ⁡(ind⁡Z)​hm=ℤ​hm/ℤ​n​hm,\CH^{m}X=\mathbb{Z}h^{m}/A_{0}=\mathbb{Z}h^{m}/\mathbb{Z}(\ind Z)h^{m}=\mathbb{Z}h^{m}/\mathbb{Z}nh^{m},

while for i=m−1i=m-1, this gives

Pic⁡X≅CH1⁡X=ℤ​h/Am−1=ℤ​h/ℤ⁡[Z]=ℤ​h/ℤ​d​h.\Pic X\cong\CH^{1}X=\mathbb{Z}h/A_{m-1}=\mathbb{Z}h/\mathbb{Z}[Z]=\mathbb{Z}h/\mathbb{Z}dh.

Thus, LL is dd-torsion. Since c1​(𝒪ℙm​(1))=hc_{1}({\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{m}}(1))=h, we have

c1​(L)m=hm|X=hm+ℤ​n​hm,c_{1}(L)^{m}=h^{m}|_{X}=h^{m}+\mathbb{Z}nh^{m},

which means that c1​(L)mc_{1}(L)^{m} has order nn in CHm⁡X\CH^{m}X.

(ii) The scheme X′X^{\prime} is affine because the morphism X′→XX^{\prime}\to X is affine and XX is affine. We continue to use the notation from the proof of (i).

By [18, Ex. 2.6.3], for every ii, there is an exact sequence

CHi−1⁡X→c1​(𝒪⁡(ℓ)|X)CHi⁡X→p∗CHi⁡X′→0.\CH^{i-1}X\xrightarrow{c_{1}({\mathcal{O}}(\ell)|_{X})}\CH^{i}X\xrightarrow{p^{*}}\CH^{i}X^{\prime}\to 0.

Since c1​(𝒪⁡(ℓ)|X)=ℓ​h+ℤ​d​hc_{1}({\mathcal{O}}(\ell)|_{X})=\ell h+\mathbb{Z}dh, this allows us to identify CHi⁡X′\CH^{i}X^{\prime} with

CHi⁡X/(ℓ​h)​CHi−1​X=ℤ​hi/(Am−i+ℤ​ℓ​hi).\CH^{i}X/(\ell h)\CH^{i-1}X=\mathbb{Z}h^{i}/(A_{m-i}+\mathbb{Z}\ell h^{i}).

and p∗p^{*} with the quotient map. In particular, Pic⁡X′=CH1⁡X′\Pic X^{\prime}=\CH^{1}X^{\prime} is ℓ\ell-torsion, hence LL is ℓ\ell-torsion. Furthermore,

CHm⁡X′=ℤ​hm/⟨n​hm,ℓ​hm⟩=ℤ​hm/ℤ​gcd⁡(n,ℓ)​hm.\CH^{m}X^{\prime}=\mathbb{Z}h^{m}/\left<nh^{m},\ell h^{m}\right>=\mathbb{Z}h^{m}/\mathbb{Z}\gcd(n,\ell)h^{m}.

Now, by (i),

c1​(L′)m=p∗​(c1​(L)m)=p∗​(hm+ℤ​n​hm)=hm+ℤ​gcd⁡(n,ℓ)​hmc_{1}(L^{\prime})^{m}=p^{*}(c_{1}(L)^{m})=p^{*}(h^{m}+\mathbb{Z}nh^{m})=h^{m}+\mathbb{Z}\gcd(n,\ell)h^{m}

and it follows that c1​(L′)mc_{1}(L^{\prime})^{m} has order gcd⁡(n,ℓ)\gcd(n,\ell) in CHm⁡X′\CH^{m}X^{\prime}. ∎

Remark 5.8.

In an earlier version of this text, we gave a different construction of ℓ\ell-torsion (ℓ>1\ell>1) line bundles LL with c1​(L)m≠0c_{1}(L)^{m}\neq 0. However, we found out that complements of high-index hypersurfaces in projective spaces give rise to examples of smaller dimension.

In our original construction, we took XX to be the total space of the line bundle 𝒪⁡(−ℓ){\mathcal{O}}(-\ell) over ℙm{\mathbb{P}}^{m} minus the zero section, and LL to be the pullback of 𝒪⁡(−1){\mathcal{O}}(-1) along X→ℙmX\to{\mathbb{P}}^{m}. We then replaced XX and LL with their pullback along the standard Jouanolou device of ℙm{\mathbb{P}}^{m} [20] to make XX affine. The resulting ℓ\ell-torsion line is induced by the 𝝁ℓ{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell}-torsor 𝐆𝐋m+1/[𝐆𝐋m1]→𝐆𝐋m+1/[𝐆𝐋m𝝁ℓ]{\mathbf{GL}}_{m+1}/[\begin{smallmatrix}{\mathbf{GL}}_{m}&\\ &1\end{smallmatrix}]\to{\mathbf{GL}}_{m+1}/[\begin{smallmatrix}{\mathbf{GL}}_{m}&\\ &{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell}\end{smallmatrix}]. We omit the details as they will not be needed here; the proof that LL is ℓ\ell-torsion and c1​(L)m≠0c_{1}(L)^{m}\neq 0 is similar to the proof of Proposition 5.7(ii). (When passing to the Jouanolou device, apply [40, Tag 0GUB].)

Example 5.9.

Recall that the uu-invariant of kk, denoted u⁡(k)u(k), is the supremum of all the integers nn for which kk admits an nn-dimensional nonsingular anisotropic quadratic form. We claim that

gk​(2,m)=Gk​(2,m)=mg_{k}(2,m)=G_{k}(2,m)=m

whenever 1≤m<u⁡(k)1\leq m<u(k). In particular, if u⁡(k)=∞u(k)=\infty, e.g., if kk is real, then gk​(2,m)=Gk​(2,m)=mg_{k}(2,m)=G_{k}(2,m)=m for all mm. To see this, let q:km+1→kq:k^{m+1}\to k be an anisotropic nonsingular quadratic form, let ZZ be the quadric hypersurface q=0q=0 in ℙm{\mathbb{P}}^{m} and let X=ℙm−ZX={\mathbb{P}}^{m}-Z. Since qq is nonsingular and anisotropic, ZZ is integral, and by Springer’s Theorem [32, II, Thm. 5.3], ind⁡Z=2\ind Z=2. Proposition 5.7(i) now tells us that the line bundle 𝒪ℙm​(1)|X{\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{m}}(1)|_{X} is 22-torsion and satisfies c1​(L)m≠0c_{1}(L)^{m}\neq 0. As a result, Gk​(2,m)≤mG_{k}(2,m)\leq m, and it follows that gk​(2,m)=Gk​(2,m)=mg_{k}(2,m)=G_{k}(2,m)=m.

In the special case k=ℝk=\mathbb{R} and q⁡(x)=∑i=1m+1xi2q(x)=\sum_{i=1}^{m+1}x_{i}^{2}, the scheme XX is isomorphic to the quotient of the mm-sphere by the antipodal map, and we recover the example in Swan [42, Thm. 4].

In order to apply Proposition 5.7, we need to find integral hypersurfaces in ℙm{\mathbb{P}}^{m} having index greater than 11. Norm forms of finite field extensions give rise to such examples.

Lemma 5.10.

Let K/kK/k be a finite separable field extension of degree nn and let a∈Ka\in K be an element such that K=k⁡[a]K=k[a]. For every m∈{1,…,n−1}m\in\{1,\dots,n-1\} set Vm=span⁡{1,a,…,am}V_{m}=\Span\{1,a,\dots,a^{m}\}, and let ZmZ_{m} be the hypersurface in ℙ⁡(Vm)≅ℙm{\mathbb{P}}(V_{m})\cong{\mathbb{P}}^{m} cut by the equation NrK/k⁡(x0+x1​a+⋯+xm​am)=0\Nr_{K/k}(x_{0}+x_{1}a+\dots+x_{m}a^{m})=0. Then ZmZ_{m} is integral. Moreover, if [K:k][K:k] is a power of a prime number ℓ\ell, then ℓ|ind⁡Zm\ell\mid\ind Z_{m}.

Proof.

The fact that ZmZ_{m} is integral follows from [15, Thm. 1] and its proof.

Suppose now that [K:k]=ℓr[K:k]=\ell^{r} for a prime number ℓ\ell and r∈ℕr\in\mathbb{N}. We need to show that ℓ|ind⁡Zm\ell\mid\ind Z_{m}. Let LL be a finite kk-field with Zm​(L)≠∅Z_{m}(L)\neq\emptyset. Then the norm NL⊗kK/L:L⊗kK→LN_{L\otimes_{k}K/L}:L\otimes_{k}K\to L has a non-trivial zero. This means that L⊗kKL\otimes_{k}K is not a field. This can happen only if ℓr=[K:k]\ell^{r}=[K:k] and [L:k][L:k] are not coprime, so ℓ\ell must divide [L:k][L:k]. ∎

Corollary 5.11.

Let ℓ\ell be a prime number.

  1. (i)

    If kk admits a separable field extension of degree ℓ\ell, then Gk​(ℓ,m)=mG_{k}(\ell,m)=m for all m∈{1,…,ℓ−1}m\in\{1,\dots,\ell-1\}.

  2. (ii)

    If kk admits a separable field extension of degree ℓr\ell^{r} for some r∈ℕr\in\mathbb{N}, then Gk​(ℓ,m)≤m+1G_{k}(\ell,m)\leq m+1 for all m∈{1,…,ℓr−1}m\in\{1,\dots,\ell^{r}-1\}.

Proof.

(i) Let K/kK/k be a finite separable field extension of degree ℓ\ell. Choose a∈Ka\in K with K=k⁡[a]K=k[a], which exists by the Primitive Element Theorem, and define ZmZ_{m} as in Lemma 5.10. Then ZmZ_{m} is an integral hypersurface in ℙm{\mathbb{P}}^{m} having degree and index ℓ\ell. Proposition 5.7(i) now provides us with a line bundle bundle LL over ℙm−Zm{\mathbb{P}}^{m}-Z_{m} such that c1​(L)m≠0c_{1}(L)^{m}\neq 0, so Gk​(ℓ,m)≤mG_{k}(\ell,m)\leq m.

(ii) This similar to (i), but we use Proposition 5.7(ii) instead of part (i) of that proposition. ∎

Corollary 5.11 cannot be applied to algebraically closed fields. This is remedied by the following proposition at the cost of increasing the upper bound on Gk​(ℓ,m)G_{k}(\ell,m) by 11.

Proposition 5.12.

Let kk be a field and ℓ,m∈ℕ∪{0}\ell,m\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\} with ℓ≠1\ell\neq 1. Then Gk​(ℓ,m)≤Gk⁡(t)​(ℓ,m)+1G_{k}(\ell,m)\leq G_{k(t)}(\ell,m)+1.

Proof.

This is shown by spreading out from Spec⁡k⁡(t)\Spec k(t) to Spec⁡k⁡[t]\Spec k[t]. What we need is summarized neatly in [29, Thms. 3.2.1, 6.4.3].

In detail, let XX be a smooth affine k⁡(t)k(t)-scheme of dimension Gk⁡(t)​(ℓ,m)G_{k(t)}(\ell,m) carrying an ℓ\ell-torsion line bundle LL with c1​(L)m≠0c_{1}(L)^{m}\neq 0. Put S=Spec⁡k⁡[t]S=\Spec k[t] and let ξ=Spec⁡k⁡(t)\xi=\Spec k(t) be the generic point of SS. By [29, Thm. 3.2.1], there is a dense open subscheme UU of SS and a UU-scheme of finite presentation YY such that Yξ=XY_{\xi}=X. Moreover, by shrinking UU if necessary, we may further assume that Y→UY\to U is smooth and UU is affine. Thus, YY is a smooth affine kk-scheme. By [29, Thm. 6.4.3] (applied to G=𝐆𝐦G={\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}), we can shrink UU even further to guarantee that there exists an ℓ\ell-torsion line bundle MM on YY such that the pullback of MM along ξ→S\xi\to S is LL. The map X=Yξ→YX=Y_{\xi}\to Y induces a ring homomorphism CH∗⁡Y→CH∗⁡X\CH^{*}Y\to\CH^{*}X which is compatible with Chern classes [11, §52F]. Thus, the image of c1​(M)mc_{1}(M)^{m} in CH∗⁡X\CH^{*}X is c1​(L)mc_{1}(L)^{m}, which is nonzero. We conclude that Gk​(ℓ,m)≤dimY=dimX+1=Gk⁡(t)​(ℓ,m)+1G_{k}(\ell,m)\leq\dim Y=\dim X+1=G_{k(t)}(\ell,m)+1. ∎

Corollary 5.13.

Let kk be a field and let m,ℓ∈ℕ∪{0}m,\ell\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\} with ℓ≠1\ell\neq 1. Then Gk​(ℓ,m)≤m+2G_{k}(\ell,m)\leq m+2. When ℓ\ell has a prime divisor greater than mm (this holds when ℓ=0\ell=0), we moreover have Gk​(ℓ,m)≤m+1G_{k}(\ell,m)\leq m+1.

Proof.

Let K=k⁡(t)K=k(t). By Proposition 5.12, it is enough to show that GK​(ℓ,m)≤mG_{K}(\ell,m)\leq m when ℓ\ell has a prime divisor p>mp>m, and GK​(ℓ,m)≤m+1G_{K}(\ell,m)\leq m+1 in general. Observe that KK has a separable field extension of degree nn for every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, for instance, K⁡[x]/(xn−t​x−t)K[x]/(x^{n}-tx-t). Letting nn range over the powers of some prime divisor pp of ℓ\ell and applying Corollary 5.11(ii) gives GK​(ℓ,m)≤GK​(p,m)≤m+1G_{K}(\ell,m)\leq G_{K}(p,m)\leq m+1. If ℓ\ell has a prime divisor pp greater than mm, then applying Corollary 5.11(i) to that divisor gives GK​(ℓ,m)≤GK​(p,m)=mG_{K}(\ell,m)\leq G_{K}(p,m)=m. ∎

Remark 5.14.

Suppose that k=ℂk=\mathbb{C}. In [28], Paulsen conjectured the following:

  1. (P)

    Let m,d∈ℕm,d\in\mathbb{N} with d≥2​md\geq 2m and let YY be a very general hypersurface of degree dd in ℙm+1{\mathbb{P}}^{m+1}. Then the degree of every positive-dimensional closed subvariety ZZ of YY is divisible by dd.

The case m=3m=3 is a famous conjecture of Griffiths–Harris. We shall consider conjecture (P) for a general field kk.

Fix kk and mm. If Paulsen’s conjecture holds for every dd sufficiently large, then Gk​(ℓ,m)≤m+1G_{k}(\ell,m)\leq m+1 for every ℓ∈ℕ−{1}\ell\in\mathbb{N}-\{1\}. Indeed, choose r∈ℕr\in\mathbb{N} coprime to ℓ\ell such that (P) holds with d=ℓ​rd=\ell r, let YY be as in the conjecture and let X=ℙm+1−YX={\mathbb{P}}^{m+1}-Y. With notation as in the proof of Proposition 5.7, the conjecture says that for every 0≤i<m0\leq i<m, the image of the pushforward map CHi⁡Y→CHi+1⁡ℙm+1=ℤ​hi+1\CH^{i}Y\to\CH^{i+1}{\mathbb{P}}^{m+1}=\mathbb{Z}h^{i+1} is ℤi+1​d​hi+1\mathbb{Z}^{i+1}dh^{i+1}. The cokernel of this map is CHi+1⁡X\CH^{i+1}X, so it can be identified with ℤ​hi+1/ℤ​d​hi+1\mathbb{Z}h^{i+1}/\mathbb{Z}dh^{i+1} whenever 0≤i<m0\leq i<m. Now put L=𝒪ℙm+1​(r)|XL={\mathcal{O}}_{{\mathbb{P}}^{m+1}}(r)|_{X}. Then c1​(L)=r​h+d​h​ℤc_{1}(L)=rh+dh\mathbb{Z} while c1​(L)m=rm​hm+ℤ​d​hmc_{1}(L)^{m}=r^{m}h^{m}+\mathbb{Z}dh^{m}. Since ℓ​r=d\ell r=d and gcd⁡(ℓ,r)=1\gcd(\ell,r)=1, this means that LL is ℓ\ell-torsion and c1​(L)m≠0c_{1}(L)^{m}\neq 0. As XX is affine of dimension m+1m+1, we conclude that Gk​(ℓ,m)≤m+1G_{k}(\ell,m)\leq m+1.

When k=ℂk=\mathbb{C}, Paulsen [28, Thm. 3, Prop. 7] showed that for every mm there is a subset S⊆ℕS\subseteq\mathbb{N} of positive density such that (P) holds for every d∈Sd\in S. The set SS consists of numbers that are coprime to m!m!, and together with the argument of the last paragraph, it can be used to show that Gℂ​(ℓ,m)≤m+1G_{\mathbb{C}}(\ell,m)\leq m+1 if all the prime factors of ℓ\ell are greater than mm. However, this is already included in Corollary 5.13.

The next results give bounds on Gk​(0,m)G_{k}(0,m). They rely on deeper results of Bloch, Mohan Kumar, Murthy, Szpiro, Roitman and Roy appearing in [26], [6], [27].

Proposition 5.15 ([6, §5]).

For every m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N}, there is t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N} such that for every field kk with char⁡k=0\Char k=0 and trdegℚ​k≥t\mathrm{trdeg}_{\mathbb{Q}}k\geq t, we have Gk​(0,m)=mG_{k}(0,m)=m.

Proof.

Suppose first that kk is algebraically closed and uncountable. We will use several results from [6] that are stated over k=ℂk=\mathbb{C}, but as is evident from their proofs, are actually true over any uncountable algebraically closed field of characteristic 00. Following the beginning of the proof of [6, Thm. 5.8], let C1,…,CmC_{1},\dots,C_{m} be elliptic curves over kk, put Y=C1×⋯×CmY=C_{1}\times\dots\times C_{m} and let XX be a dense open affine subset of YY. Then H0​(Y,Λm​ΩY)≠0{\mathrm{H}}^{0}(Y,\Lambda^{m}\Omega_{Y})\neq 0. By [6, Lem. 5.2], this implies that CHm⁡(X)≠0\CH^{m}(X)\neq 0 (our assumptions on kk are needed here). Moreover, CHm⁡(X)\CH^{m}(X) is clearly generated by products of the form α1⋯αm\alpha_{1}\cdots\alpha_{m} with α1,…,αm∈CH1⁡(X)\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{m}\in\CH^{1}(X) (because this also holds for YY). Thus, by [6, Lem. 5.6], there is a line bundle LL over XX such that c1​(L)m≠0c_{1}(L)^{m}\neq 0. It follows that Gk​(0,m)=mG_{k}(0,m)=m.

Suppose now that kk is uncountable. Let X′X^{\prime} and L′L^{\prime} be the XX and LL constructed in the last paragraph for the field k¯\overline{k}. As in the proof of Proposition 5.12, there is a finite extension k1k_{1} of kk such that X′X^{\prime} and L′L^{\prime} descend to k1k_{1}, i.e., there is a smooth affine k1k_{1}-scheme XX and a line bundle LL over XX such that X×k1k¯=X′X\times_{k_{1}}\overline{k}=X^{\prime} and L′L^{\prime} is the pullback of LL along X′→XX^{\prime}\to X. The image of c1​(L)mc_{1}(L)^{m} under CHm⁡X→CHm⁡X′\CH^{m}X\to\CH^{m}X^{\prime} is c1​(L′)m≠0c_{1}(L^{\prime})^{m}\neq 0, so we must have c1​(L)m≠0c_{1}(L)^{m}\neq 0. As XX is a smooth affine kk-scheme of dimension mm, it follows that Gk​(0,m)=mG_{k}(0,m)=m.

Finally, suppose that kk is countable. Let X′X^{\prime} and L′L^{\prime} be the XX and LL constructed for the field ℂ\mathbb{C}. Again, there is a finitely generated ℚ\mathbb{Q}-field k0k_{0}, such that X′X^{\prime} descends to a smooth affine k0k_{0}-scheme X0X_{0} and L′L^{\prime} descends to a line bundle L0L_{0} over X0X_{0}. We take t:=trdegℚ​k0t:=\mathrm{trdeg}_{\mathbb{Q}}k_{0}. If trdegℚ​k≥t=trdegℚ​k0\mathrm{trdeg}_{\mathbb{Q}}k\geq t=\mathrm{trdeg}_{\mathbb{Q}}k_{0}, then there is a finite extension k1k_{1} of kk that is isomorphic to a field lying between k0k_{0} and ℂ\mathbb{C}. Identifying k1k_{1} with that field, put X=X0×k0k1X=X_{0}\times_{k_{0}}k_{1} (viewed as a kk-scheme) and let LL to be the pullback of L0L_{0} along X→X0X\to X_{0}. As before, c1​(L)m≠0c_{1}(L)^{m}\neq 0 (because its image in CHm⁡X′\CH^{m}X^{\prime} is c1​(L′)m≠0c_{1}(L^{\prime})^{m}\neq 0) and Gk​(0,m)=mG_{k}(0,m)=m. ∎

Remark 5.16.

The example in [6, Thm. 5.8] relies on a criterion of Roitman [6, Lem. 5.2] for showing that the group of 00-cycles on a complete kk-variety YY is infinite dimensional in the sense that there is no closed subvariety Z⊊YZ\subsetneq Y such that CH0⁡(Z)→CH0⁡(Y)\CH_{0}(Z)\to\CH_{0}(Y) is surjective. This criterion, originally proved for k=ℂk=\mathbb{C}, requires kk that is uncountable algebraically closed of characteristic 00.

V. Srinivas pointed out to us that Bloch gave an analogue of Roitman’s result for uncountable fields of positive characteristic using ℓ\ell-adic cohomology [5, Thm. 1A.6, Ex. 1A.7] (see also [4, Prop. 1]). Moreover, it seems likely that with some work, this result could be applied to the example in [6, Thm. 5.8]. We therefore expect that Proposition 5.15 also holds in positive characteristic.

Proposition 5.17.

Let m∈ℕ−{1}m\in\mathbb{N}-\{1\} and let pp be a prime number. Then G𝔽¯p​(0,m)=m+1G_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}(0,m)=m+1.

Proof.

Since G𝔽¯p​(0,m)≤m+1G_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}(0,m)\leq m+1 (Corollary 5.13), it is enough to prove that if X=Spec⁡AX=\Spec A is a smooth affine 𝔽¯p\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}-scheme of dimension mm, then CHm⁡X=0\CH^{m}X=0. By [26, Thm. 3.6], every closed point of XX is a complete intersection, and by [27, Cor. 3.4, Thm. 2.14ii)], this means that CHm⁡X≅Fm​K0​(A)=0\CH^{m}X\cong F^{m}K_{0}(A)=0. ∎

Remark 5.18.

The characteristic-00 counterpart of Proposition 5.17, i.e., whether Gℚ¯​(0,m)=m+1G_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(0,m)=m+1 for all m≥2m\geq 2, is related to the Bloch–Beilinson conjecture. Indeed, in some formulations, e.g. [21, p. 157] or [39, Cnj. 7.4, Cnj. 7.7], the conjecture may be stated as follows:

  1. (BB)

    For every smooth affine ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}}-variety XX of dimension m≥2m\geq 2, we have CHm⁡X=0\CH^{m}X=0.

If this holds, then we must have Gℚ¯​(0,m)≥m+1G_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(0,m)\geq m+1, and then equality holds by Corollary 5.13.

We conclude our discussion of Gk​(ℓ,m)G_{k}(\ell,m) with the following theorem, which implies Theorem 5.1.

Theorem 5.19.

Let kk be a field and let ℓ,m\ell,m be non-negative integers with ℓ≠1\ell\neq 1.

  1. (i)

    Gk​(ℓ,0)=0G_{k}(\ell,0)=0 and Gk​(ℓ,1)=1G_{k}(\ell,1)=1.

  2. (ii)

    Gk​(ℓ,m)∈{m,m+1,m+2}G_{k}(\ell,m)\in\{m,m+1,m+2\}.

  3. (iii)

    If ℓ\ell is divisible by a prime number greater than mm (e.g. ℓ=0\ell=0), then Gk​(ℓ,m)∈{m,m+1}G_{k}(\ell,m)\in\{m,m+1\}.

  4. (iv)

    If kk is algebraically closed, m>1m>1 and ℓ>0\ell>0, then Gk​(ℓ,m)≥m+1G_{k}(\ell,m)\geq m+1. Equality holds if ℓ\ell is moreover divisible by a prime number greater than mm.

  5. (v)

    If char⁡k=0\Char k=0 and trdegℚ​k\mathrm{trdeg}_{\mathbb{Q}}k is infinite, then Gk​(0,m)=mG_{k}(0,m)=m.

  6. (vi)

    G𝔽¯p​(0,m)=m+1G_{\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}}(0,m)=m+1 for every prime p>0p>0 and m≥2m\geq 2.

Proof.

(ii), (iii), (iv), (v), (vi) follow from Corollary 5.13 and Propositions 5.6, 5.15, 5.17. As for (i), that Gk​(ℓ,0)=0G_{k}(\ell,0)=0 is clear — take LL to be the trivial line bundle on Spec⁡k\Spec k. To show that Gk​(ℓ,1)=1G_{k}(\ell,1)=1, note first that there is a finite separable kk-field k1k_{1} and an ordinary elliptic curve C1C_{1} over k1k_{1}. (Indeed, all elliptic curves are ordinary in characteristic 00, and if p=char⁡k>0p=\Char k>0, then any elliptic curve with jj-invariant not lying in 𝔽p2\mathbb{F}_{p^{2}} is ordinary.) Since C1C_{1} is ordinary, there is a finite separable k1k_{1}-field k2k_{2} and P∈C1​(k2)P\in C_{1}(k_{2}) of order ℓ\ell [40, Tag 03RP]. Let C2=C1×k1k2C_{2}=C_{1}\times_{k_{1}}k_{2} and let OO be the trivial point of C2C_{2}. Then X:=C2−{O}X:=C_{2}-\{O\} is affine and smooth over kk, and [P]∈CH1⁡X≅Pic⁡X[P]\in\CH^{1}X\cong\Pic X is the 11-st Chern class of a nontrivial ℓ\ell-torsion line bundle LL over XX. ∎

Proof of Theorem 5.1.

Thanks to Corollary 5.5 and Lemma 5.2, this follows from Theorem 5.19. ∎

6. Main Results

We finally prove Theorems 1.1 and 1.2. We will use the invariant gk​(ℓ,m)g_{k}(\ell,m) defined in Section 5. Recall from Theorem 5.1 that gk​(ℓ,m)∈{m,m+1,m+2}g_{k}(\ell,m)\in\{m,m+1,m+2\} and gk​(0,m)∈{m,m+1}g_{k}(0,m)\in\{m,m+1\}.

We derive Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 from the following theorem.

Theorem 6.1.

Let kk be a field, let GG be a closed subgroup of 𝐆𝐋n{\mathbf{GL}}_{n} (n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}), let E→XE\to X be a GG-torsor with XX a quasi-compact kk-scheme and let VV be the vector bundle over XX corresponding to the 𝐆𝐋n{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}-torsor E×G𝐆𝐋n→XE\times^{G}{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}\to X. Let mm be a non-negative integer such that one of the following holds:

  1. (1)

    m≥n​spl⁡Vm\geq n\spl V, or

  2. (2)

    m≥n⁡(dimX+1)m\geq n(\dim X+1) and XX is quasi-projective over a field.

Suppose further that there is a kk-field KK and ℓ∈ℕ−{1}\ell\in\mathbb{N}-\{1\} such that 𝛍ℓ,K{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell,K} embeds in GKG_{K}. Then there is a smooth affine KK-scheme X′X^{\prime} of dimension gK​(ℓ,m)g_{K}(\ell,m) carrying a GG-torsor that is not a specialization of E→XE\to X.

Proof.

Assumption (2) implies (1) by Proposition 4.2. By the definition of g:=gK​(ℓ,m)g:=g_{K}(\ell,m), there is a gg-dimensional smooth affine KK-scheme X′X^{\prime} carrying an ℓ\ell-torsion line bundle L′L^{\prime} such that gen⁡(L′)>m\gen(L^{\prime})>m. For the sake of contradiction, suppose that E→XE\to X specializes to every GG-torsor over X′X^{\prime}, i.e., E→XE\to X is weakly versal for the class of kk-schemes {X′}\{X^{\prime}\}. Then by [12, Prop. 5.5], the GKG_{K}-torsor EK→XKE_{K}\to X_{K} is weakly versal for the class of KK-schemes {X′}\{X^{\prime}\}. Since GKG_{K} contains a copy of 𝝁ℓ,K{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell,K}, Theorem 4.5(i) tells us that every ℓ\ell-torsion line bundle over X′X^{\prime} can be generated by n​spl⁡(VK)≤n​spl⁡Vn\spl(V_{K})\leq n\spl V elements. But that is absurd because L′L^{\prime} was chosen so that gen⁡(L′)>m≥n​spl⁡V\gen(L^{\prime})>m\geq n\spl V. We therefore conclude that E→XE\to X does not specialize to all GG-torsors over X′X^{\prime}. ∎

We also have the following variant of Theorem 6.1 which gives a slightly better upper bound on dimX′\dim X^{\prime} when GKG_{K} contains a copy of 𝐆𝐦,K{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m},{K}}.

Theorem 6.2.

Let kk, nn, GG, E→XE\to X, VV and mm be as in Theorem 6.1. Suppose further that there is a kk-field KK such that 𝐆𝐦,K{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m},{K}} embeds in GKG_{K} and the characters of 𝐆𝐦,K{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m},{K}} occurring in the representation 𝐆𝐦,K→GK→𝐆𝐋n,K{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m},{K}}\to G_{K}\to{\mathbf{GL}}_{n,K} include the identity character or x↦x−1x\mapsto x^{-1}. Then there is a smooth affine KK-scheme X′X^{\prime} of dimension gK​(0,m)g_{K}(0,m) carrying a GG-torsor E′→X′E^{\prime}\to X^{\prime} that is not a specialization of E→XE\to X.

Proof.

This is similar to the proof of Theorem 6.1, except L′L^{\prime} is not necessarily torsion and one uses part (ii) of Theorem 4.5 instead of part (i). ∎

We can now prove Theorems 1.1 and 1.2 as well as a few improvements.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

The implication (b)⟹\implies(a) is clear and (c)⟹\implies(b) is a special case of [12, Thm. 10.1]. It remains to show that (a)⟹\implies(c), that is, we need to show that if XX is a quasi-compact kk-scheme and E→XE\to X is a GG-torsor that is weakly versal for all finite type regular affine kk-schemes, then GG is unipotent.

For the sake of contradiction, suppose that GG is not unipotent. By Theorem 3.6(ii), Gk¯G_{\overline{k}} contains a copy of 𝝁ℓ,k¯{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell,\overline{k}} for some ℓ>1\ell>1. This means that there is a finite-dimensional kk-field KK such that GKG_{K} contains a copy of 𝝁ℓ,K{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell,K}. Theorem 6.1 now gives us a GG-torsor E′→X′E^{\prime}\to X^{\prime}, where X′X^{\prime} is a smooth affine KK-scheme, which is not a specialization of E→XE\to X. Since X′X^{\prime} is regular affine and also of finite type over kk, this contradicts our assumption on E→XE\to X. We conclude that GG must be unipotent. ∎

Theorem 6.3.

Let kk be a field and GG be an affine algebraic kk-group. Suppose that GG is connected, or kk is perfect. Then the conditions of Theorem 1.1 are also equivalent to:

  1. (a+)

    there exists a GG-torsor over a quasi-compact kk-scheme that is weakly versal for all smooth affine kk-schemes.

Proof.

As in the proof of Theorem 1.1, it is enough to prove that (a+) implies that GG is unipotent. Suppose that (a+) holds but GG is not unipotent. Then, as in the proof of Theorem 1.1, given a finite-dimensional kk-field KK such that GKG_{K} contains a copy of 𝝁ℓ,K{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell,K} with ℓ>1\ell>1, we could use Theorem 6.1 to get a smooth affine KK-scheme X′X^{\prime} and a GG-torsor E′→X′E^{\prime}\to X^{\prime} that is not a specialization of E→XE\to X. We will reach the desired contradiction by showing that KK can be taken to be separable over kk, and thus X′X^{\prime} is smooth over kk.

When kk is perfect, we could simply take KK to be the kk-field from the proof Theorem 1.1. If GG is connected, then Theorem 3.6(i) tells us that GG contains a nontrivial multiplicative group MM. In this case, take KK to be a finite separable kk-field such that MKM_{K} is diagonalizable. ∎

Theorem 1.2 is part (i) of the following theorem.

Theorem 6.4.

Let GG be a non-unipotent algebraic subgroup of the algebraic kk-group 𝐆𝐋n{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}, let XX be a dd-dimensional kk-scheme that is quasi-projective over a field and let E→XE\to X be a GG-torsor. Then:

  1. (i)

    E→XE\to X is not weakly versal for the class of finite type regular affine kk-schemes of dimension ≤n⁡(d+1)+2\leq n(d+1)+2.

  2. (ii)
