    If kk is perfect or GG is connected, then E→XE\to X is not weakly versal for the class of smooth affine kk-schemes of dimension ≤n⁡(d+1)+2\leq n(d+1)+2.

  3. (iii)

    If GG contains a nontrivial torus, then E→XE\to X is not weakly versal for the class of smooth affine kk-schemes of dimension ≤n⁡(d+1)+1\leq n(d+1)+1.

  4. (iv)

    If char⁡k=0\Char k=0, trdegℚ​k\mathrm{trdeg}_{\mathbb{Q}}k is infinite and Gk¯G_{\overline{k}} contains a copy of 𝐆𝐦,k¯{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m},{\overline{k}}} such that characters of the representation 𝐆𝐦,k¯→Gk¯→𝐆𝐋n,k¯{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m},{\overline{k}}}\to G_{\overline{k}}\to{\mathbf{GL}}_{n,\overline{k}} include the identity character or x↦x−1x\mapsto x^{-1}, then E→XE\to X is not weakly versal for the class of smooth affine kk-schemes of dimension ≤n⁡(d+1)\leq n(d+1).

Proof.

(i) By Theorem 3.6(ii), there is a a finite dimensional kk-field KK such that GKG_{K} contains a copy of 𝝁ℓ,K{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell,K} for some ℓ>1\ell>1. Put m=n⁡(d+1)m=n(d+1) and let E′→X′E^{\prime}\to X^{\prime} be the GG-torsor guaranteed in Theorem 6.1. Then E→XE\to X does not specialize to E′→X′E^{\prime}\to X^{\prime}. Since dimX′=gK​(ℓ,m)≤m+2\dim X^{\prime}=g_{K}(\ell,m)\leq m+2, we conclude that E→XE\to X is not weakly versal for finite type regular affine kk-schemes of dimension ≤n⁡(d+1)+2\leq n(d+1)+2.

(ii) As in the proof of Theorem 6.3, there is a separable finite-dimensional kk-field KK such that GKG_{K} contains a copy of 𝝁ℓ,K{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell,K} for some ℓ>1\ell>1. Proceed as in (i) using this KK. The scheme X′X^{\prime} is smooth over kk because it is smooth over KK and KK is smooth over kk.

(iii) Let TT be a nontrivial subtorus of GG and let KK be a finite separable kk-field splitting TT. Then GKG_{K} contains a copy 𝐆𝐦,K{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m},{K}}. Let ℓ\ell be a prime number greater than m:=n⁡(d+1)m:=n(d+1). Then GKG_{K} contains a copy of of 𝝁ℓ,K{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\ell,K}. Proceed as in (i), but note that gK​(ℓ,m)≤m+1g_{K}(\ell,m)\leq m+1 by Theorem 5.1(iii).

(iv) The assumption on GG implies that there is a finite separable kk-field KK such that GKG_{K} contains a copy of 𝐆𝐦,K{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m},{K}} and the characters of the representation 𝐆𝐦,K→GK→𝐆𝐋n,K{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m},{K}}\to G_{K}\to{\mathbf{GL}}_{n,K} include x↦xx\mapsto x or x↦x−1x\mapsto x^{-1}. We now argue as in (i) using Theorem 6.2 instead of Theorem 6.1. Theorem 5.1(v) tells us that gK​(0,m)=mg_{K}(0,m)=m. ∎

An immediate application of Theorem 6.4 is the following.

Corollary 6.5.

Let GG be a non-unipotent algebraic subgroup of the algebraic kk-group 𝐆𝐋n{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}. Then there exists a finite type regular affine kk-scheme of dimension n+2n+2 carrying a non-trivial GG-torsor E→XE\to X. If kk is perfect or GG is connected, then XX can be taken to be smooth as well.

Proof.

Apply Theorem 6.4 to the GG-torsor G→Spec⁡kG\to\Spec k. ∎

As we noted in the introduction, this result can be significantly improved in terms of dimension when GG contains a nontrivial torus; this will be shown in the next section. Another way to strengthen Corollary 6.5 is the following.

Corollary 6.6.

Let HH be an algebraic subgroup of the algebraic kk-group 𝐆𝐋n{\mathbf{GL}}_{n} and let GG be a non-unipotent algebraic subgroup of HH. Then there exists a GG-torsor E→XE\to X, with XX a finite type regular affine kk-scheme such that the HH-torsor E×GH→XE\times^{G}H\to X is nontrivial. Furthermore, XX can be taken so that dimX≤n⁡(dimH−dimG+1)+2\dim X\leq n(\dim H-\dim G+1)+2.

The corollary is obtained by applying Theorem 6.4 to the GG-torsor H→H/GH\to H/G, so improvements analogous to parts (ii), (iii), (iv) of Theorem 6.4 hold. We leave it to the reader to work them out explicitly.

Proof.

Let XX be a kk-scheme. It is well-known that there is a short exact sequence of pointed sets

(H/G)​(X)→𝛼Hfppf1​(X,G)→𝛽Hfppf1​(X,H)(H/G)(X)\xrightarrow{\alpha}\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{fppf}}(X,G)\xrightarrow{\beta}\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\mathrm{fppf}}(X,H)

in which α\alpha takes an XX-point p:X→H/Gp:X\to H/G to the cohomology class of the GG-torsor obtained by base-changing H→H/GH\to H/G along pp, and β\beta takes the cohomology class of a GG-torsor E→XE\to X to the cohomology class of E×GH→XE\times^{G}H\to X. From the sequence we see that every GG-torsor E→XE\to X such that E×GH→XE\times^{G}H\to X is trivial is a specialization of the GG-torsor H→H/GH\to H/G. Thus, for any GG-torsor E→XE\to X that is a not a specialization of H→H/GH\to H/G, the extension E×GH→XE\times^{G}H\to X is a nontrivial HH-torsor. With this observation at hand, the corollary follows by applying Theorem 6.4 to the GG-torsor H→H/GH\to H/G. (Note that H/GH/G is quasi-projective.) ∎

7. Non-Trivial Torsors

We finish with using results from Sections 4 and 5 to prove Theorem 1.3. This will improve Corollary 6.6 for algebraic groups containing a nontrivial torus.

We will derive Theorem 1.3 from a slightly more general result. To phrase it, we introduce a variation of the invariant Gk​(ℓ,m)G_{k}(\ell,m) considered in Section 5. For every m∈ℕ∪{0}m\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}, let

G~k​(m)\tilde{G}_{k}(m)

denote the smallest d∈ℕ∪{0}d\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\} such that for every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, there is a smooth affine dd-dimensional kk-scheme and a line bundle LL such that n⋅c1​(L)m≠0n\cdot c_{1}(L)^{m}\neq 0 in CHm⁡X\CH^{m}X.

Theorem 7.1.

Let GG be an affine algebraic group over kk containing a nontrivial torus (resp. central torus). Then there exists a smooth affine kk-scheme of dimension at most G~k​(2)\tilde{G}_{k}(2) (resp. G~k​(1)\tilde{G}_{k}(1)) carrying a non-trivial GG-torsor.

Proof of Theorem 1.3 using Theorem 7.1.

It is enough to show that G~k​(m)≤m+1\tilde{G}_{k}(m)\leq m+1, G~k​(1)≤1\tilde{G}_{k}(1)\leq 1 and, provided that char⁡k=0\Char k=0 and trdegℚ​k\mathrm{trdeg}_{\mathbb{Q}}k is infinite, G~k​(m)≤m\tilde{G}_{k}(m)\leq m.

For the first inequality, given n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, choose some prime number ℓ\ell larger than mm and nn. By Theorem 5.19(iii), there is a smooth affine kk-scheme XX with dimX≤m+1\dim X\leq m+1 and an ℓ\ell-torsion line bundle LL such that c1​(L)m≠0c_{1}(L)^{m}\neq 0. Since c1​(L)c_{1}(L) is ℓ\ell-torsion and ℓ∤n\ell\nmid n, we must have n⋅c1​(L)m≠0n\cdot c_{1}(L)^{m}\neq 0. Thus, G~k​(m)≤m+1\tilde{G}_{k}(m)\leq m+1.

The second inequality is shown similarly, using Theorem 5.19(i).

For the last inequality, write K=k¯K=\overline{k}. We may assume that m>1m>1 as we already showed that G~k​(1)≤1\tilde{G}_{k}(1)\leq 1. By Theorem 5.19(v), there is a smooth affine KK-scheme XX with dimX=m\dim X=m and a line bundle LL such that c1​(L)m≠0c_{1}(L)^{m}\neq 0. By a result of Murthy [27, Thms. 2.11, 2.14], CHm⁡X\CH^{m}X is torsion-free (here we need m>1m>1 and KK to be algebraically closed). Thus, n⋅c1​(L)m≠0n\cdot c_{1}(L)^{m}\neq 0 for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. The KK-scheme XX and the line bundle LL descend to some finite-dimensional kk-field, which is separable over kk because char⁡k=0\Char k=0, hence G~k​(m)≤m\tilde{G}_{k}(m)\leq m. ∎

We turn to prove Theorem 7.1. We first prove the following lemma.

Lemma 7.2.

Let σ1,σ2:ℤn→ℤ\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}:\mathbb{Z}^{n}\to\mathbb{Z} be the first and second elementary symmetric functions. Then for every x∈ℤn−{0}x\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}-\{0\}, either σ1​(x)≠0\sigma_{1}(x)\neq 0 or σ2​(x)≠0\sigma_{2}(x)\neq 0.

Proof.

Write x=(x1,…,xn)x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n}). We have σ1​(x)2−2​σ2​(x)=σ1​(x12,…,xn2)≠0\sigma_{1}(x)^{2}-2\sigma_{2}(x)=\sigma_{1}(x_{1}^{2},\dots,x_{n}^{2})\neq 0, so at least one of σ1​(x)\sigma_{1}(x), σ2​(x)\sigma_{2}(x) must be nonzero. ∎

Proof of Theorem 7.1.

Let TT be a nontrivial torus contained in GG (resp. the center of GG). It is harmless to base-change from kk to a finite separable extension splitting TT. We may therefore assume that GG (resp. its center) contains a copy of 𝐆𝐦{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}.

Choose a homomorphism G→𝐆𝐋nG\to{\mathbf{GL}}_{n} such that the composition φ:𝐆𝐦→G→𝐆𝐋n\varphi:{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}\to G\to{\mathbf{GL}}_{n} is nontrivial, e.g., a faithful representation of GG. It is enough to show that there is a smooth affine kk-scheme XX with dimX≤G~k​(2)\dim X\leq\tilde{G}_{k}(2) (resp. dimX≤G~k​(1)\dim X\leq\tilde{G}_{k}(1)) and a 𝐆𝐦{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}-torsor EE such that E×𝐆𝐦𝐆𝐋nE\times^{{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}}{\mathbf{GL}}_{n} is a nontrivial 𝐆𝐋n{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}-torsor. Indeed, since E×𝐆𝐦𝐆𝐋n=(E×𝐆𝐦G)×G𝐆𝐋nE\times^{{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}}{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}=(E\times^{{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}}G)\times^{G}{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}, this would force E×𝐆𝐦G→XE\times^{{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}}G\to X to be a nontrivial GG-torsor.

Let {x↦xai}i=1n\{x\mapsto x^{a_{i}}\}_{i=1}^{n} be the characters of the representation φ:𝐆𝐦→𝐆𝐋n\varphi:{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}\to{\mathbf{GL}}_{n} (with multiplicities). We observed in the proof of Lemma 4.4 that if LL is the line bundle corresponding to EE, then the vector bundle corresponding to E×𝐆𝐦𝐆𝐋nE\times^{{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}}{\mathbf{GL}}_{n} is V:=L⊗a1⊕⋯⊕L⊗anV:=L^{\otimes a_{1}}\oplus\dots\oplus L^{\otimes a_{n}}. Thus, the total Chern class of VV is c(V)=c(L⊗a1)⋯c(L⊗an)=∏i=1n(1+aic1(L))c(V)=c(L^{\otimes a_{1}})\cdots c(L^{\otimes a_{n}})=\prod_{i=1}^{n}(1+a_{i}c_{1}(L)). Writing a=(a1,…,an)∈ℤna=(a_{1},\dots,a_{n})\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}, this means that

ci​(V)=σi​(a)​c1​(L)ic_{i}(V)=\sigma_{i}(a)c_{1}(L)^{i}

for all i∈{1,…,n}i\in\{1,\dots,n\}, where σi\sigma_{i} is the ii-th elementary symmetric function. Since a≠0a\neq 0, Lemma 7.2 tells us that σm​(a)≠0\sigma_{m}(a)\neq 0 for some m∈{1,2}m\in\{1,2\}.

We now choose XX to be a G~k​(m)\tilde{G}_{k}(m)-dimensional smooth affine kk-scheme carrying a line bundle LL with σm​(a)⋅c1​(L)m≠0\sigma_{m}(a)\cdot c_{1}(L)^{m}\neq 0. By what we just showed, cm​(V)=σm​(a)⋅c1​(L)m≠0c_{m}(V)=\sigma_{m}(a)\cdot c_{1}(L)^{m}\neq 0 and it follows that E×𝐆𝐦𝐆𝐋n→XE\times^{{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}}{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}\to X is a nontrivial 𝐆𝐋n{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}-torsor. As G~k​(m)≤G~k​(2)\tilde{G}_{k}(m)\leq\tilde{G}_{k}(2) (because m∈{1,2}m\in\{1,2\}), this proves the theorem when TT is not assumed to be central in GG.

When TT is contained in the center of GG, we choose φ:G→𝐆𝐋n\varphi:G\to{\mathbf{GL}}_{n} in such a way that 𝐆𝐦{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}} is also mapped into the center of 𝐆𝐋n{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}. (Such representations exist, e.g., start with a faithful representation VV of GG, chose a nontrivial character χ:𝐆𝐦→𝐆𝐦\chi:{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}\to{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}} occurring in 𝐆𝐦→G→𝐆𝐋⁡(V){\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}\to G\to{\mathbf{GL}}(V) and take the eigenspace VχV_{\chi}.) Then there is a∈ℤ−{0}a\in\mathbb{Z}-\{0\} such that a1=⋯=an=aa_{1}=\dots=a_{n}=a. This means that σ1​(a)=n​a≠0\sigma_{1}(a)=na\neq 0, so we can take m=1m=1 and get dimX≤G~k​(1)\dim X\leq\tilde{G}_{k}(1). ∎

We finish with showing that there are algebraic groups for which Theorem 1.3 is the best possible result in terms of dimension.

Example 7.3.

Consider the algebraic kk-group 𝐒𝐋n{\mathbf{SL}}_{n} (n>1n>1). By Theorem 1.3, there is a smooth affine kk-scheme XX with dimX≤3\dim X\leq 3 carrying a nontrivial 𝐒𝐋n{\mathbf{SL}}_{n}-torsor. Provided that char⁡k=0\Char k=0 and trdegℚ​k\mathrm{trdeg}_{\mathbb{Q}}k is infinite, we can even take XX with dimX=2\dim X=2.

On the other hand, every 𝐒𝐋n{\mathbf{SL}}_{n}-torsor over an affine noetherian scheme of dimension smaller than 22 is trivial. Indeed, it is well-known that there is a bijection between isomorphism classes of 𝐒𝐋n{\mathbf{SL}}_{n}-torsors over XX and rank-nn vector bundles XX with trivial determinant, in which the trivial torsor corresponds to 𝒪Xn{\mathcal{O}}_{X}^{n}. (This can be seen, for instance, by inspecting the long fppf cohomology exact sequence associated to the short exact sequence 𝐒𝐋n↪𝐆𝐋n→det→𝐆𝐦{\mathbf{SL}}_{n}\hookrightarrow{\mathbf{GL}}_{n}\xrightarrow{\det}\mathrel{\mkern-14.0mu}\rightarrow{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{m}}.) Let EE be an 𝐒𝐋n{\mathbf{SL}}_{n}-torsor over a noetherian affine kk-scheme XX with dimX<2\dim X<2 and let VV be the corresponding vector bundle with det(V)≅𝒪X\det(V)\cong{\mathcal{O}}_{X}. By a theorem of Bass–Serre [3, Thm. 8.2] (see also [33, Thm. 1]), our assumptions on XX imply that V≅𝒪Xn−1⊕LV\cong{\mathcal{O}}^{n-1}_{X}\oplus L for some line bundle LL, so det(V)≅L\det(V)\cong L. Since we also have det(V)≅𝒪X\det(V)\cong{\mathcal{O}}_{X}, it follows that V≅𝒪XnV\cong{\mathcal{O}}_{X}^{n} and E→XE\to X is trivial.

For algebraically closed fields, we can make Example 7.3 more precise and even extend it to semisimple groups of type G2G_{2}. The latter case is essentially due to Asok, Hoyois and Wendt [1].

Proposition 7.4.

Let kk be an algebraically closed field, let XX be a smooth irreducible affine kk-scheme with dimX<3\dim X<3, let n>1n>1 and let GG denote the semisimple algebraic kk-group of type G2G_{2}. Then the following are equivalent:

  1. (a)

    CH2⁡X=0\CH^{2}X=0;

  2. (b)

    every 𝐒𝐋n{\mathbf{SL}}_{n}-torsor over XX is trivial;

  3. (c)

    every GG-torsor over XX is trivial.

Proof.

We start with showing that (a)⇔\iff(c). The field k⁡(X)k(X) has cohomological dimension at most 22, and thus every GG-torsor over XX is trivial over the generic point [36, Apx. 2.3.3]. Thus, by [1, Thm. 1], CH2⁡X\CH^{2}X is in bijection with Hfppf1​(X,G){\mathrm{H}}^{1}_{\mathrm{fppf}}(X,G) and the equivalence is immediate.

We proceed with showing that (a)⇔\iff(b). Suppose first that (a) holds. Let EE be an 𝐒𝐋n{\mathbf{SL}}_{n}-torsor over XX and let VV be its corresponding vector bundle as in Example 7.3. We have seen that E→XE\to X is trivial when dimX<2\dim X<2, so assume dimX=2\dim X=2. By the Bass–Serre Theorem [33, Thm. 1], V≅V′⊕𝒪Xn−2V\cong V^{\prime}\oplus{\mathcal{O}}_{X}^{n-2} for some rank-22 vector bundle V′V^{\prime}. Since CH2⁡X=0\CH^{2}X=0, we have c2​(V′)=0c_{2}(V^{\prime})=0. By a theorem of Murthy [27, Thm. 3.8], this means that there is a line bundle LL such that V′≅L⊕𝒪XV^{\prime}\cong L\oplus{\mathcal{O}}_{X} and as in Example 7.3, we get that E→XE\to X is trivial.

Suppose now that (b) holds. If dimX<2\dim X<2, then CH2⁡X=0\CH^{2}X=0, so assume dimX=2\dim X=2. Let c∈CH2⁡Xc\in\CH^{2}X. As explained in [25, §1, a)], there is a rank-22 vector bundle V′V^{\prime} with c1​(V′)=0c_{1}(V^{\prime})=0 and c2​(V′)=cc_{2}(V^{\prime})=c. Since c1​(V′)=c1​(det(V′))=0c_{1}(V^{\prime})=c_{1}(\det(V^{\prime}))=0, it follows that det(V′)≅𝒪X\det(V^{\prime})\cong{\mathcal{O}}_{X}. Let E→XE\to X be the 𝐒𝐋n{\mathbf{SL}}_{n}-torsor corresponding to V:=V′⊕𝒪Xn−2V:=V^{\prime}\oplus{\mathcal{O}}_{X}^{n-2}. By (c), EE is trivial, so VV is free, and it follows that c=c2​(V′)=c2​(V)=0c=c_{2}(V^{\prime})=c_{2}(V)=0. ∎

Corollary 7.5.

Let pp be a prime number and let GG be a semisimple simply connected algebraic 𝔽¯p\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}-group of type AnA_{n} or G2G_{2}. Then every GG-torsor over a smooth affine 𝔽¯p\overline{\mathbb{F}}_{p}-scheme XX of dimension <3<3 is trivial.

Proof.

We observed in the proof of Proposition 5.17 that CH2⁡X=0\CH^{2}X=0, so this follows from Proposition 7.4. ∎

Remark 7.6.

Let GG be a semisimple simply connected algebraic group over ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}} of type AnA_{n} or G2G_{2}. By Proposition 7.4, the statement that every GG-torsor over a smooth affine 22-dimensional ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}}-scheme is trivial is equivalent to the Bloch–Beilinson conjecture for surfaces [21, p. 157, (b)].
